Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's economic Dracula has stalked his latest victim. The so-called king of GST, Michael Wilson, has embraced the queen, Kim Campbell. Is this the kiss of death?
This architect of Conservative economic policies which have devastated this country is the person who has brought us the GST, which we know is the most inefficient and ineffective tax ever introduced by any government. He has thrown his support behind the defence minister. She welcomes his support and vows to continue the Conservative legacy. This legacy is bleeding Canadians dry.
He has said she is the candidate closest to his vision. What have the last nine years of Conservative vision brought us? A made-in-Canada recession, trade policies which destroy Canadian jobs, high unemployment, bankruptcies, high real interest rates, and a growing number of poor and homeless.
Canadians have had enough of Conservative hypocrisy. Liberals will form the next government and will bring back hope and opportunities for Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I watched an American news broadcast with interest this morning as it outlined the U.S. proposal to station American soldiers at the border between Macedonia and
Serbia. Their purpose would be to monitor the UN sanctions.
This article caught my attention because I recently talked with a group of very capable soldiers stationed at that exact border crossing. Their mission was also to monitor UN sanctions.
However they were not Americans but were Canadians. They have been stationed at this very dangerous location for some time. Not only were they Canadians but some were from my own province of Nova Scotia.
From the news broadcast one would think that the U.S. was leading the way when in fact it is still talking while Canadians are acting.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year a tragic helicopter accident in Niagara Falls claimed four lives. In response to that, to the petitions and to the complaints of hundreds of people in the city, Niagara Falls now has the most regulated airspace in the country.
We now control the number of helicopters in the sky at any one time. The altitude of all flying aircraft is restricted. Communications procedures between helicopters are now mandatory. Helicopters must stay within the restricted airspace and cannot fly over any residential area in the city of Niagara Falls.
In the immediate future we will put all air traffic on radar 24 hours a day. We will know if anyone tries to go outside the flight path.
These measures will ensure that every visitor and resident of Niagara Falls is safe from overhead traffic. In addition, I want everyone in our city to be able to enjoy their residences in peace.
If these measures are not enough I will want more because the days of a free-for-all over the skies of Niagara Falls are over. The message is simple: Either play by the rules or do not play at all.

May 12, 1993

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians understand that global climate change threatens food supply, forests, the Arctic and coastal communities with rising sea levels.
Some countries have decided to reduce carbon dioxide emissions to meet this threat. Three years ago Canada promised only to freeze greenhouse gas emissions at 1990 levels by the year 2000. Three years have gone by and the government still lacks an action plan to achieve such a freeze.
This government's snail paced response to global climate change also puts Canada at a competitive disadvantage. The government should recognize that countries with strong economies, such as Germany and Japan, have the highest energy efficiency and the lowest per capita carbon dioxide emissions.
If the government were serious about responding to the threat of global warming, it would wake up and produce a sustainable long-term energy policy with meaningful reductions in carbon dioxide emissions.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is Canada Health Day. The theme this year is Caring about Health: Everyone's Responsibility.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is today building on that theme to launch Healthy Canada, a call to all Canadians to be more actively involved in their own health and in the health of their families and communities.
We know that health involves more than medical interventions and more than health care. Each of us has benefited from the care extended by another when we were ill. Such care or compassion can be instrumental in restoring health. Today is an appropriate time to remember that health is a shared responsibility and a shared benefit. Today is also a time to recognize and take pride in a health system that ranks among the finest in the world.
I would like to thank the Canadian Hospital Association and the Canadian Public Health Association for sponsoring this day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week is National Nursing Week in Canada and today is International Nurses Day.
This day is being recognized by nurses in the Public Service of Canada who are profiling Jeanne Mance, Canada's first nurse, with the re-instalment of a plaque in her honour at the Jeanne Mance Building of Health and Welfare Canada.
As the nation pays verbal tribute to the dedication and professionalism of nurses, it should be remembered that this is one of those pink collar ghettos in which people of competence and professionalism are paid far less than their work is worth.
For instance, in the Public Service of Canada 1,500 nurses are owed over $37 million in back pay equity. The injustice goes on.
In the Department of National Defence the minister has failed to take any action on the clear discrimination of $15,000 a year against nurses, dietitians and therapists as compared to engineers, architects and chemists who are mostly male, surprisingly.
Therefore let International Nurses Day not be a day of nice words and no action but one that really recognizes the value of the work of nurses in the paycheque.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make the House aware of the totally unacceptable delays in unemployment insurance appeals at the umpire level.
Illustrating the gravity of the situation is the fact that 4,358 cases remain unheard at this level of appeal. There are simply too many cases for too few federal judges to address the backlog. Recent legislative changes in immigration and unemployment insurance will only make a bad situation much worse.
I cite one example to demonstrate the extreme delays suffered by workers who feel the system has treated them unfairly. Hundreds of workers still await a hearing date with the umpire as a result of a labour dispute at Algoma Steel in 1990. I am told the hearing could be held this fall, some three years later.
Surely any reasonable person would realize the system is failing. I ask the minister to take full responsibility and, more important, immediate action.

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to bring to the attention of the House an amendment to the health of animals regulations which is going to have a serious impact on Canadian bee keepers.
The border was closed to the importation of honey bees into Canada from the United States because of two pests infecting American bees. Now the ban is being lifted against the advice of Canadian bee keepers and provincial authorities. Even the Americans cannot understand why Canada would lift the ban.
The Department of Agriculture claims that imported bees can be virtually pest-free with the use of chemicals during shipment. The fact is that chemicals will render only 93 per cent protection and 93 per cent is not good enough. The department also claims that there is no chemical residue in the honey subsequently produced, but honey processors disagree.
On behalf of the Canadian bee industry I ask that this regulatory amendment be reversed and the importation ban be extended until such time as the bees can be guaranteed to be 100 per cent pest-free.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. It has to do with the horrific situation in Bosnia.
Today in London, England, the Prime Minister said that the Security Council of the United Nations should only authorize the use of force under certain conditions.
Does Canada plan to use our troops in an offensive operation in Bosnia? Will the government agree to consult the people of Canada through Parliament before committing our troops to a new role of that nature?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

May 12, 1993

Oral Questions
Obviously there would be discussion among the Canadian people but the ultimate decision as the hon. member knows is the government's in terms of decisions of this nature.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

I went to Bosnia and to Croatia in order to discuss the situation and all of its aspects with the people there, Canadians and others who are on the ground. I am also going to committee this afternoon where I can give a more detailed answer to the kind of question the hon. member has presented.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister.
In the speech that was given by the Prime Minister this morning he said that the rejection of the Vance-Owen plan by the Bosnian Serbs had clearly put the ball back in our court. He listed a number of options that the international community must now consider: safe havens, sealing of the borders, ending of the arms embargo or air strikes.
What he did not say is which of these actions Canada prefers and whether we will participate in these actions. Given that these options have been discussed now for weeks in different areas of the international community, is it not about time the government was prepared to spell out clearly in this Parliament exactly what our position is to stop the suffering and horror in Bosnia?

I am sure the hon. member will be at the committee this afternoon and I can go into some considerable detail on this very topic. I simply do not understand the line of questioning given that this is coming before the member's own committee this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind the minister that this is the entire Parliament representing all Canadians from coast to coast to coast. It is not a committee and Canadians deserve to have some serious answers.
Last night Canadian troops came under serious fire in Srebrenica. Unfortunately one of our troops was hurt. The Bosnian ambassador has now called for the withdrawal of peacekeepers so that other action can be taken. The Prime Minister said this morning that humanitarian assistance and military enforcement were incompatible.
Was our Prime Minister this morning saying that the government is now considering withdrawing our troops from the exposed positions they now occupy in Srebrenica and in other areas, or is it considering changing the nature of the role of our troops so that they will

May 12, 1993

undertake a different mandate to help bring the stoppage of the violence and horror that are taking place every single minute of every single day in Bosnia?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously members of this House and certainly of this government are very sorry about the injury to the soldier yesterday. Of course he was not the first. We had a soldier injured in Croatia not very long ago as well. These are always incidents that the military try to avoid by minimizing the risk on the ground.
In terms of the incompatibility of enforcement and the delivery of humanitarian assistance, yes, these two objectives would be very difficult to put in place. Neither one was being advocated, by the way, and neither was the withdrawal of our troops.
What was being laid out were the options if the international community chose to go a certain way. The Prime Minister also pointed out that the choices our government as well as other governments face all have downsides.
At the moment the humanitarian deliveries are providing some value within this situation and lives have been saved. The question facing all of us is: If the objective changes then it will probably not be possible to do that any longer and would we make the situation better or worse?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Hardly a day goes by now in Canada where we do not see another major lay-off and more Canadians out of work. It really has become a very serious crisis. Unemployment has not gone down; indeed it has gone up.
In a season when in fact we should see employment going up, just this past week we saw the Scarborough GM plant close with 3,000 workers out of work. Air Canada announced that 1,200 more jobs were cut. Yesterday workers at a 76-year old Jergens plant found
out that it was shutting down. To no one's surprise, Nationair declared bankruptcy today.
Given the seriousness of the situation, what is the Deputy Prime Minister prepared to do to give some hope to these Canadians? Those with jobs are feeling very insecure and are wondering if they will be next. What kind of plan will he bring forward in the last remaining weeks of this government to make sure he can get Canadians back working? Then the countiy would really work.

speechtext: Some of the items, reductions in personal income tax, the two-year special home buyers plan, a reduction in the manufacturing and processing tax rate, the increase in the capital cost allowance, streamlining research and development, no new taxes, no tax increases, a number of measures to strengthen the infrastructure, more measures for training and skills upgrading, are starting to take hold.

A particularly concerning statistic is that of youth unemployment which is officially 18 per cent and unofficially higher. The minister talks about seeing things improving but the unemployment rate has gone up. It has gone up higher for young people and for women.
May 12, 1993

Oral Questions
The government's own projections project no change in years to come. I therefore ask the minister: In response to the young people, many of whom are now finishing school, what plan does he have to give them hope that they will be able to use the skills they have developed? Where are the jobs for the young people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the composite leading indicator represents a broad spectrum of the Canadian economy. It is a broad measurement that indicates the economy is indeed expanding.
The hon. member talks about unemployment. Employment in the manufacturing sector is up by 28,000, up by 4 per cent or 70,000 new jobs in the last six months. She and everyone else in this House knows that the manufacturing sector has indeed had the greatest challenge in terms of restructuring and adjusting to the competitive realities of the international marketplace.
Housing starts are up as recently announced. Surveys indicate that manufacturing will increase by some 33 per cent. Exports are strong. Construction spending is up. Infrastructure projects are starting to come on stream. The energy sector has been revitalized, having increased its activity by 100 per cent over last year. Retail sales are up. Consumer confidence is up. Business confidence is up. These are the kinds of indicators reflected in the composite index.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the minister visit any unemployment office, any line-up for student employment, and he will see the real world out there. People are not finding jobs.
All the job losses I just mentioned were caused by free trade and deregulation. These policies were bad when they were adopted, they are bad policies today and they will still be bad tomorrow.
Instead of rushing into NAFTA and dragging its feet on the crisis in the air transportation industry, why doesn't the government do the opposite: accelerate the process for dealing with the crisis in the air transportation industry and slow down on NAFTA?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, exports to the United States are up in my home province of Alberta by something like 40 per cent. Exports in British Columbia are up by about 20 per cent. Exports in Saskatchewan are up by about 25 per cent. In Manitoba they are up by about 25 per cent. In Ontario they are up by close to 20 per cent.
When the hon. member criticizes the free trade agreement, she knows as well as anyone else in this House that the economy is working itself out of the recession as a result of the strong performance in exports, as a result of the strong performance in productivity, as a result of the restructuring and the adjustment that have taken place. That is a fact of life.
Some of her friends in the New Democratic Party are indeed finding that out. Ask Mr. Harcourt, ask Mr. Rae, ask Mr. Romanow. If the realities of the marketplace are not there then they have to be adjusted.

I want to point out to the hon. member that the Canadian soldiers who were going into Srebrenica were very much looking forward to this assignment. The morale was high. They knew they were on an important mission and their commander who was leading them, Lieutenant-Colonel Geburt who was going with them into Srebrenica, felt that the mission they had there was doable.
I had long discussions with General Gaudreau while I was there. Of course there are risks. There are also risks to our soldiers in Croatia who were being fired on three days before I was there in the western sector of Croatia.
We recognize there are dangers. We recognize there are risks. That is the nature of what is happening in Bosnia. What we have tried to do as a government and certainly what the Canadian military is trying to do is reduce those risks as far as possible given the nature of the assignment. I can assure our families of that.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to introduce this bill that would amend the Young Offenders Act.
The purpose of this particular bill is threefold. First, it would lower the age limits that define a young offender. A young offender would be defined as a young person between the ages of 10 and 15. As a result, 16 and 17 year olds would be responsible for their criminal acts and prosecuted in adult court. As well, the lower age limit of a young offender would be reduced from 12 to 10 years of age. Second, the bill would increase the maximum penalty for first or second degree murder to 10 years from the current 5-year maximum. Third, the bill would allow for the publication of the name of the young offender after the offender's second conviction for an indictable offence.

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, May 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-89, an act to amend the Investment Canada Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.

Madam Speaker, as I was saying yesterday before we concluded, I realize that the government will use its majority to put through these amendments to the Investment Canada Act. The operative agency is Investment Canada. Nevertheless I felt it was important we were on record flagging our concerns about the way the government has altered the approach to foreign investment from that of the previous government.
The example I used yesterday was the example of Mercedes-Benz and Freightliner. Here was an example
May 12, 1993

where Mercedes-Benz wanted to have more retail outlets for its cars in Canada. I remember in 1981-82 we said to Mercedes-Benz: "There is no way you are going to sell more of your product in Canada unless you give us a firm commitment that you are going to maintain the manufacturing of the Freightliner trucks in British Columbia".
As I stated yesterday Mercedes-Benz really did not want that imposition by the Foreign Investment Review Agency, FIRA. The company fought it and we maintained our ground as a government. Ultimately the company honoured the commitment to Freightliner.
Today Freightliner, which operates out of St. Thomas, Ontario, has about 600 manufacturing jobs. I guess it was last year that the former president of Mercedes-Benz told me when I ran into him at a luncheon in Toronto: "I was certainly mad at the Foreign Investment Review Agency in 1981-82, but I can report to you today that Freightliner is now one of the most profitable divisions in Canada under the Daimler-Benz or Mercedes-Benz umbrella".
That is for me the way the Investment Canada operation should function. It should be functioning in that way. When people want to come to Canada to do business it should be challenging them to set up manufacturing concerns. In fact in my view it should be giving them firm advice that this is the way we expect them to do business in Canada. We do not just want them to come here, set up a warehouse, hire an ad agency, market their product and have a few sales people. We want them to come here and do some research and development and some manufacturing.
What has happened in the country in the last few years is that we have just seen a retreat from research and development and a retreat from manufacturing. I believe that this all goes back to chapter 14 of the free trade agreement.
Essentially I am a free trader. I am not against Canada trading around the world. I have always had a pretty progressive attitude toward trade. We have to have an understanding and a regulation by sector and there has to be some sense of fair play in this.
The Prime Minister even said this before he was elected in 1983 in my riding when he was campaigning to
Government Orders
be the leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. He made the statement that unfettered, unlimited free trade with the Americans would be no different than a mouse sleeping next to an elephant. Somehow he forgot that commitment he made in 1983 and here we have chapter 14 of the free trade agreement.
I want to be on the record. This is not the first time for me. When I was campaigning in the last election I flagged this chapter as the one area of the free trade agreement that was ultimately going to lead to a Government of Canada calling in on the abrogation clause.
I really wish Canadians could go to their libraries or call their local MPs and ask them for a copy of chapter 14 of the free trade agreement, which is the chapter that really deals with the sovereignty of this country. It is the chapter that is directly related to this bill, Bill C-89, with the amendments to the Investment Canada Act. It has to do with the whole approach in terms of when people come to this country and the terms and conditions under which they do business.
I want to quote directly from article 1402 of this free trade agreement that says basically: "Subject to paragraph 3 each party shall accord to persons of the other party treatment no less favourable than that accorded in like circumstance to its persons with respect to the measures covered by this chapter".
Point two says: "The treatment accorded by a party under paragraph 1 shall mean with respect to a province or a state treatment no less favourable than the most favourable treatment accorded by such province or state in like circumstances to persons of the party of which it forms a part".
My concern is that there have been too many instances where we have not been given equal treatment under this section of the free trade agreement.
Of course the government agency or body that has been responsible for making sure that that type of treatment is being maintained is the Investment Canada section of the Government of Canada. When I hear of instances like the General Motors van plant in Scarborough shutting down and moving to Flint and about organizations that are shutting down and retreating to the United States, then I get very concerned that chapter 14 of the free trade agreement is not working the way it was intended to work.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
I am concerned about the government agency Investment Canada.
I have always been a supporter of the notion that we need foreign investment in this country. We need an exchange of technology. We need manufacturing. We want companies to come here and set up their manufacturing concerns. I really think our negotiating skills in making sure part of the package is that they manufacture here have wilted away. We do not seem to have the same political will today to meet that objective as we did a few years ago.
Today we debate amendments to Bill C-89 and the government will put this bill through with its majority. I want to go on record as saying that I have concerns about the direction Investment Canada has been taking in the last few years. I especially have concerns about the fact that chapter fourteen of the free trade agreement has really not met the stated objective of the government's campaign in 1988.
The minister of trade and the Minister of Finance will stand and give all kinds of examples where certain sectors of the economy have surges in exports. I happen to think the main reasons those exports are up has to do with not only our levels of productivity but also our rate of exchange in terms of dollars. I still believe if we had mandated companies to keep their manufacturing businesses in Canada they still could have maintained their profitability. We still could have maintained those jobs and the economy would have been much healthier than what we are dealing with today.

Madam Speaker, I have a newspaper article in my hand from the October 26 edition of The Nikkei Weekly which I think is of profound importance. It concerns Bill C-89 which we are discussing today.
If I may, I would like to quote from part of it. It is not very long. The heading of the article is "NAFTA impacting investment strategy". Now that is of course in Japan. The subheading is that "62 per cent of subsidiaries in U.S. are attracted to Mexico, survey shows". The article goes on, datelined New York: "More than 60 per cent of Japanese companies operating in the U.S. believe that the North American free trade agreement increases Mexico's appeal as an investment site, according to a recent survey by Nihon Keizai Shinbun".
"Most respondents, presidents and vice-presidents of 269 U.S. subsidiaries of Japanese firms listed on the
Tokyo-Osaka Stock Exchanges, expect NAFTA to have a major impact on their North American business strategies".
More than half the respondents, 52.4 per cent, answered yes to the question: "Do you think NAFTA promotes regionalism or protectionism?" That is 52 per cent; only 14 per cent said no.
I might interject that about a week and a half ago a former deputy minister of NUT, which is the minister for international trade in Tokyo, was in this building. He indicated to members present that the business community in Japan has profound concerns about NAFTA. Those concerns are completely consistent with the survey I just mentioned where more than half of the executives interviewed in this particular poll thought that NAFTA promoted regionalism or protectionism.
If I may, I am going to read from the article:
NAFTA will directly influence Japanese companies by demanding that goods qualifying for tariff-free trade have a higher local content ratio. In the case of automobiles for example, the local content ratio would rise to 62.5 per cent.
I wish I had heard my friend or the minister opposite speak on that issue. Perhaps they will speak to it in Question Period.
At present under the U.S.-Canada free trade pact, the ratio is 50 per cent. In the poll, 54.3 per cent of respondents said that higher local content requirements would have a major impact on their future management while 41.3 per cent said they would have little or no effect. That split in opinion may stem from the fact that local content ratios directly affect manufacturers but leave service industries virtually untouched.
Asked if the agreement would necessitate changes in the investment strategies in the three countries, 23.8 per cent said
"yes"-
These are Japanese business executives.
38.7 per cent said "no" and 35.7 per cent were not sure. Of those in agreement, 84.4 per cent said that they would consider Mexico as an investment site compared with 32.8 per cent for the U.S. and 15.6 per cent for this country of Canada.
Most respondents said that they will maintain the status quo in their Canadian investments, since Canada and the U.S. have already implemented a free trade agreement.
NAFTA will make Mexico a more attractive place to invest according to 62.1 per cent of respondents largely because Mexico will have to relax its numerous restrictions on foreign investment.

Many electrical goods manufacturers have already relocated their U.S. production bases to Mexico to take advantage of the less expensive labour. Mexico now appears likely to become the strongest candidate of the three for Japanese manufacturers setting up in North America.
Maybe I should repeat that so I can stress it for the minister.
Mexico now appears likely to become the strongest candidate of the three for Japanese manufacturers setting up in North America.
Currently most Japanese companies' Mexican plants are concentrated in the Maquiladora district near the U.S. border.
That is fairly clear.

Finally if I may read a related article underneath the one I just quoted from headed "Bank of Tokyo bullish on Mexico":
Mexico will grow in importance as a hub for Japanese manufacturing in the wake of the North American Free Trade Agreement, according to Kaoru Hayama, Bank of Tokyo's senior managing director in charge of overseas operations.
"Manufacturers that export to the U.S. market would obviously benefit by locating in Mexico where their products crossing the border north would not be subject to tariffs", he said in a recent interview. "Of course, the number of new factories built in Mexico by Japanese companies will grow".
Hayama said that companies that already have operations in Mexico will find it easier to open sales routes throughout North America.
"Moreover, as Central and South American countries move toward freer trade, some are expected to join NAFTA, making it possible to cultivate their markets as well" Hayama said. "This is the reason the automobile industry and others are moving towards expanding their production bases in Mexico".
With NAFTA in place, Hayama said: "The first thing that comes to mind is companies with factories in the U.S. and Canada closing them down and relocating to Mexico".
He acknowledged that this would stir negative reactions in the U.S. and Canada. Hayama added: 'Another option would be to move factories in Southeast Asian countries to Mexico. This trend can already be seen in the textile industry".
Hayama said that companies with factories scattered throughout Latin America are likely to concentrate production in Mexico".
I wish every member of the House could read this article. I am afraid it is an article published in Japan that most of us will not see. I would be interested to see if the
Government Orders
Minister for International Trade has any comment on it. It seems to me, and I think Japanese business leaders have confirmed this to many audiences, that the Mexican manufacturing economy will benefit enormously from NAFTA and Bill C-89.
What about the 27 million people who the minister of trade and I are supposed to represent in this country? What about the minister's constituents? I gather he is not running again. What about the constituents of all of us here who depend on us to protect the Canadian national interest? Do we have so little regard for our duties to our constituents that we are prepared to put through any bill?
I have no doubt the vast source of manufacturing investment-I mention the car industry but there are many others-in Japan and the South Pacific is going to see NAFTA and Bill C-89 as simply ways of making Mexico the place to get 75-cent an hour labour to compete with $12 or $15 an hour labour in Canada. One cannot live in Calgary or Edmonton on a wage of 75 cents an hour. The minister may think people can and he may have studied economics-in fact, one of his professors told me he studied under him a long time ago like I did-but the trouble is that wages tend to equalize and our wages are going to equalize down.

Madam Speaker, I heard the previous Liberal member of the House of Commons speak about free trade and NAFTA and why he now opposes it. One of the reasons he opposes it is because of the low wages in Mexico.
I remember a few years ago when he was on the opposite side of the House and voted for the free trade agreement. We warned there were a number of counties in the United States which were doing all sorts of things to induce Canadian factories to come to those states.
We have seen examples time after time. They offer very low taxes and advertise that they are states with no minimum wage requirements. There is high productivity but almost no protection for the workers and there is subsidized or free land.

Madam Speaker, I did vote for the free trade agreement. I wrote about it in a book. I have written many articles about it and given many speeches.
I thought it would be good for Canada as a whole. I particularly thought it would be good for western Canada. It has been good for some industries in western Canada. There is no doubt about that. The cattle industry is very pleased with it. The petrochemical and oil and gas industries are very pleased with it, but I am a Canadian and I see that thousands and thousands of manufacturing jobs have been lost. If he looks at some of the other industries he is talking about, they are not remotely concerned with the free trade agreement. Some of them are even excluded from the free trade agreement.
I think at least we should be able to stick to the facts in this argument. Why would the hon. member insist on equating automotive issues with the free trade agreement when he knows that is not conceivably possible?

Madam Speaker, I have read each of the articles of the free trade agreement from stem to stem. I would be surprised, knowing the hon. member, if he has read it. Perhaps when he gets up next time he will tell the House if he has read it all.
May 12, 1993
Yes, I have.
He does not seem to be displaying very much knowledge about the auto pact part of the free trade agreement.
The hon. member was not on the committee. I was.
The NAFTA, as the member will know, increases local production to 62.5 per cent of local content.
Good thing.

I do not think the member from Guelph was here when I quoted some figures before so I will quote a couple of them again to him. This is an article from The Nikkei Weekly of Japan dated October 26, 1992:
NAFTA will make Mexico a more attractive place to invest, according to 62 per cent of the respondents-
These are business executives in Japan:
-	largely because Mexico will have to relax its numerous restrictions on foreign investment.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: You are over your head.

Michael, if I am over my head, you sank a long time ago.
Mr. Hayama, the managing director of the Bank of Tokyo, is quoted in the article:
Mexico will grow in importance as a hub for Japanese manufacturing in the wake of the North American free trade agreement.
"With NAFTA in place" Flayama said, "the first thing that comes to mind is companies with factories in the U.S. and Canada closing them down and -
-to the member from Guelph-
-	relocating to Mexico". He acknowledged that this would stir negative reactions in the U.S. and Canada.
Well it will stir negative reactions on this side of the House including our friends from the New Democratic Party and among members' constituents.
However those hon. members just do not get it. Where are these pages who are with us today going to work when this government is finished its work? Are these brilliant minds going to work in Mexico? The Minister for International Trade and the member from Guelph just do not get it.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, we get it. It is interesting that the hon. member does not really reply to my question about the free trade agreement and the auto pact.
It is clear the hon. member does not understand the auto pact. Apparently he has never understood it. If he looked at the auto pact rules, he would find that again we are so far above auto pact limits that we would have to close down General Motors and probably Chrysler as well to come down to the auto pact limits.
Why does the hon. member object to the 62.5 per cent? Why does he not want more North American content than the 50 per cent? I do not think he even understands what the issue is with respect to the old content rule. It is simple.
Surely we are better off with a 62.5 per cent content rule than with a 50 per cent content rule because more work will be done in North America. Maybe he wants it done in Japan, I do not know.

I will give the member a little history lesson.
When the auto pact was first passed, Mr. Diefenbaker was the leader of the hon. member's party. Neither the hon. member nor I was here; it was a long time ago. Mr. Diefenbaker was trying to decide whether his party would oppose the auto pact including its production guarantees for Canada, a fairly important factor at the time and now.
A friend of mine was in Windsor at the time. Mr. Diefenbaker and he were talking on the phone and he said: "You know, Mr. Diefenbaker, the train keeps taking loads of new Canadian cars over to the United States". I guess he and a lot of others persuaded Mr. Diefenbaker that maybe he should not oppose the auto pact.
The auto pact was brought in by this group here a bit before the member's time. There were production guarantees in the auto pact. How does the member explain the fact that last week we had how many thousands of people lose their jobs in Scarborough at the profitable van plant there?
Does the member not understand that the eight million of us who live in western Canada would like to attract investment from Japan, Korea, Taiwan and many other countries that this Euro-centric bunch over here does not even know about?

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
I am sorry, the Minister for International Trade took a trip to Asia. Anyway, if the member did not grasp what I was saying before when quoting the official from the Bank of Tokyo, I will give it to him one more time: "Companies with factories in the U.S. and Canada are closing them down and relocating to Mexico". They are very smart business people in Japan. I do not think the member from Guelph gets it, nor would he if I talked for an hour.

Madam Speaker, I found the last debate somewhat interesting.
I heard a Liberal Party member who when he was a member of the Conservative Party, of course, supported this legislation. Now that he is a Liberal, he has learned that he is against the legislation. Then again, to be Liberal is to be very flexible about your principles and your ideas.
However this is a very serious issue. We can take a look around the world at the present time to realize we are not talking about whether Canada is a more competitive country than the United States or Mexico, or whether Canadians have better skills than workers in those countries. We are talking about who really makes the decisions about where our economic growth will or will not occur.
It does not really matter to most of the corporations whether they produce goods in Canada, the United States or Mexico, or whether they provide services from any of those nations. We can have the most skilled, the best educated and the most productive workers, but if for some reason there is a corporate decision to build a large plant in Mexico, that is what will be done. Evidence was presented in debate earlier today that the Scarborough plant was profitable. It was a cash cow for General Motors, but that did not prevent it from closing down that operation.
We know, as was just quoted, that a lot of Japanese investors are looking at the North American free trade agreement and saying: "Hey, we should set up plants in Mexico". Why? Because they would have access to the United States and Canadian markets and would not have to pay our wages. They would not have to be worried about our environmental standards. They would not have to be worried about our workers' compensation.
They would not have to be worried about occupational health and safety legislation. Even if there was legislation in any of those areas we know that it would not likely be enforced.
I was part of a parliamentary delegation that went to Mexico a few years ago prior to the free trade deal being negotiated. I was amazed by the power of the party in power to change absolutely everything around to suit its agenda. We were down there to discuss issues of bilateral importance and interest, but members of that party made it sound like it was a great negotiating meeting. They actually kept the meeting going until eleven o'clock at night and had the state-controlled media claim this great victory for the Mexican party in government. All that really meant was that we agreed that we discussed certain issues, but they had that control.
One of the interesting things is that as part of that control not only did they control the media but they insisted that the state governor not have his banquet until about eleven o'clock or twelve o'clock at night. This was in order to make sure they got the maximum spin out of this meeting which really was not very important.
Just look at the events over the last few days in Thailand where over 200 workers, mostly women, in a toy factory lost their lives. They lost their lives because the owners and operators of that plant decided they wanted more productivity from those workers. They wanted to reduce theft from that shop so they locked up the fire escapes. In other words, they basically locked those workers into a death-trap. We know there are laws in Thailand saying that should not happen, but it is also obvious that those laws were not being enforced.
When we talk about the free trade agreement and when we talk about the North American free trade agreement with the U.S. and Mexico, we are not saying that Canadians are afraid to compete. We know we can compete, but we can only compete if the laws are fair and if the rules are the same in all nations.
We know that one of the great assets of the European Common Market is the fact that it does have a social contract. Its members have an understanding of how they will bring about standards among the poorer nations of the European Common Market in order that there is fair competition among those countries and a fair chance for employment by the workers in all of those countries.
May 12, 1993

There is a fair chance they will keep their factories open in all the communities of the Common Market.
When we look at the free trade agreement and the examples I gave earlier when I was questioning the Liberal member as to his fuzzy position on this issue, we know right now that American states and counties are very actively trying to take factories out of this country. We know that is happening as do those who watched an American television show yesterday afternoon. That political creature, Perot, was introduced where he brought out an ad showing how the Mexicans were even going to undercut the salaries paid in the southern states.
It would take some doing.

It would take some doing, as my colleague from Edmonton said.
Here we are with this government's concept of how we create development admitting that we are going into a very uneven playing field. We are going into a situation knowing there is almost no enforcement of the laws that do exist. Even those laws that do exist do not protect the Mexican workers, their families or the environment.
How can we say we are giving our young Canadians a chance for the future when we know that the jobs presently being done in this country will be done in other countries in the future? How can we say that we are improving the Canadian competitive position when we know that anytime we are more competitive some company for other reasons may decide to take the operations outside of Canada?
How do we know we are going to be able to predict labour standards, occupational health and safety standards, environmental standards when every time an employer can say: "If you do not do what we want, we are going to Mexico. If you do not do what we want, we are going to the southern states. If you do not do what we want, we are closing up the factory. We are closing up your town and taking away your livelihood". That is what is happening. It is happening right now in community after community right across this nation.
It is interesting that representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association want the free trade deal. They want the agreement with NAFTA. They say that it
Government Orders
will never hurt our social programs or our standard of living, that it will improve all of those things.
I remember just after the free trade agreement was signed in the late fall or early winter of 1988 a Canadian head of Ford Canada said: "Well, we may not want to operate in Ontario in the future because your workmen's compensation laws are too firm. They are too strenuous and that does not happen elsewhere".
What does that say? It says that our governments-this was not the employees, this was not negotiations-this was government legislation in the province of Ontario, long before Bob Rae was there. There was legislation that said there were certain things that should be done for workers if they were injured on the job. After the free trade agreement came in the head of Ford Canada said: "Those things are too firm. We cannot have that, otherwise we are going to take our business and do it elsewhere".
We need to have control of our own future. We will trade. We will always trade. We traded before the free trade agreement. We trade in countries now where we do not have a free trade agreement.
Let us not give up control of our own future. Let us not give up control of what we do for our young people. Let us not give up control of our resources. That is what we are doing. It does not matter how many speeches government members make, the reality is that we are giving up control of our future. We are giving up that control to foreign dominated corporations which have no sense of loyalty to this nation. They have no sense of loyalty to the communities in which they exist. They have no sense of loyalty to the workers or their families. It is going to happen time after time that Canadians will lose their jobs, lose their livelihood, and all we can say is that we told you so.
The previous speaker from the Liberal Party who was a Tory a few years ago and voted for the free trade agreement then said their party position was that they would renegotiate these agreements. You cannot renegotiate when the foundations are that rotten. You can negotiate trade agreements with other nations but to renegotiate the present free trade agreement and the NAFTA agreement is to negotiate on the basis of quicksand.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
The fundamental principles that are in both of those agreements are completely unacceptable. It is not this clause that is wrong, or that clause that is wrong. It is not this particular clause on water that is the most dangerous. It is the whole concept, not of free trade, but that all decisions will be made by transnational or multinational corporations.
That is the basic concept of this agreement. It takes away the role of the provinces. It takes away the role of the country to determine what it wants in terms of standards. It takes away the right of Canadians to determine their own future. It has taken away our social programs. It is taking away the future for our young people. It is taking away the jobs from our communities. That will continue to happen as long as we set up a situation where corporations can move, operate, produce wherever they want and there is not a damn thing Canadians can do about it.
That is what is happening. Plant after plant that closes in this country and consolidates in the United States or in the future moves to Mexico will be able to do so because we have given up our right to say: "Hold on, if you do that you lose access to the Canadian market. If you take your company, your production and move south, whether to the United States or whether it is to the southern states or whether it is to Mexico then you have lost your right to the Canadian market".
It is not right. We are not giving that right up to the United States. We are not giving that right to the Mexican government. We are giving up that right as Canadians. We are giving up that right to make those decisions that best affect our future.
We should not do that. That is why we have to oppose the NAFTA legislation. That is why we have to convince the Liberal Party that it is no to this agreement. It is no to the free trade agreement. Do not monkey around. Do not play with the crossing of fs and the dotting of is. Say no to bad legislation that is fundamentally flawed. Give Canadians the right to determine their own future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think my hon. friend overlooks certain realities. One of the realities is that the world economy is changing and competitiveness is the basis upon which industries will survive or fail. That is going to happen. That reality is
taking place throughout the world whether you have an FTA, whether you have a NAFTA or anything else. That is a reality. Look at the logic of my hon. friend's argument. Say that we are not going to bind ourselves by entering into trade agreements that give us opportunities. Those opportunities are real as reflected in the increased exports that have come under the FTA and in the increased interest that Canadian companies are having in exporting to Mexico because of the NAFTA. The logic of my friend's argument is, however, that if we are going to protect Canadian sovereignty to the nth degree then we should get out of the GATT and not sign any international covenants whether they are on human rights or anything else because they are an infringement of our sovereignty. This is the logic of my friend's argument.
Look at the legislation that is before the House today. I do not know if my friend recalls that but I think his remarks are really built on this concept of the change in the oil and gas sector that was announced initially a year ago. I wonder if my hon. friend is aware of this. Can he explain to me why, since the Minister of Energy almost a year ago announced this change, the percentage of the oil and gas sector in Canada that is owned by Canadians has increased by 4 per cent since these changes were brought in?
The logic of what he is saying, of course, is that we would be swamped and the large companies would take over the Canadian energy sector. In fact, what has happened is that the small Canadian oil and gas companies have grown and the percentage of our oil and gas industry owned by Canadians has increased by 4 per cent. Can my hon. friend explain to me why that has happened?

Madam Speaker, my friend from Edmonton East says that the figures the member is now quoting do not exist and that we do not have figures for the years he is talking about. I do not know how he can claim any increased Canadian ownership in the oil and gas field.
One of the things that concerns us is that the federal government is now talking about moving to reduce the controls that we have on foreign ownership in the oil and gas area.
May 12, 1993

Here is my concern with the remarks of the Conservative member. I never said that we were against trade. I never said that we were against the GAIT because we are not. What we are saying is that the type of trade agreement that this government has negotiated under the so-called Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the North American free trade agreement is not just the free trade of goods. If it were just that and if the Prime Minister was honest when he was having that debate in 1988 during the leadership debates then we would have a different situation.
The reality is that we have given up our right to make our own decisions in the future. Right now if we know that companies are leaving this country to go elsewhere in the world then we have some right to protect ourselves. We lose that right under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. We lose that right under the North American free trade agreement. We have basically said that the only people who have powers to make decisions in the future are the multinational corporations. We do not want the provinces to make decisions according to the government's own free trade agreement. We do not want the federal government to say that we want to have any control over drug manufacturing in the future. We leave that to the corporations. We do not want to have control over our own future.
If it wants to negotiate trade agreements then it should negotiate fair trade agreements. However, do not put in so much heavy political ideology that it prevents Canadians, either at the provincial level or the federal level and not just this generation but future generations, from making the decisions that affect our future. If it wants to have negotiations on goods then it should put together an agreement that has negotiations on goods. However, make sure that as part of that process Canadian jobs are protected and that we do not have the situation that we have at the present time where corporation after corporation after corporation is making the decision to close down Canadian operations and move those goods, plants and jobs to the United States.
Madam Speaker, the member wants to get up and debate. There was time for debate.
Mind you, that will not happen when we get to the free trade bills the week we return. We know already that this
Government Orders
government on report stage and third reading of the North American free trade agreement is only going to allow two or maybe two and a half days debate for both those stages. It is just like on second reading when it only allowed a couple of days debate on an issue that is so important to the future of this country.
Why did your people not actually participate in the committee if it was so important?

Madam Speaker, the member asks why our members did not participate. It was because we had the same situation in committee as we had in the House on second reading and we are going to have the same situation at report stage and we are going to have the same situation at third reading. As soon as that committee met and before it had heard any witnesses whatsoever, the government used its majority to say: "We will hear witnesses for thus number of days and we will finish study by Thursday".
Some study. Some public input. Some chance to have any reasonable study of legislation. All this government has done is to have closure at second reading, closure at committee, closure at report stage and closure at third reading. There was no debate. There was no public input. There was no reasoned study.
This might as well be the Russian parliament because the rights of the minority here are not protected by this majority. The rights of the public are not protected by this majority. The rights to reasoned debate are not protected by this majority in this House.
It steamrolls important legislation through the House with one objective only and that is to prevent the issue from becoming a public issue. The government prevents the public that will be concerned when it finds out about the various clauses in the North American free trade agreement to be fully informed. I must say that the government has been successful. The government has been successful not only because of its majority in this House but because the media has not been a very good public watchdog on this issue.
We hear from time to time the media saying that it is important for the public to have the right to know. During the times that I attended that committee I found one reporter and sometimes no reporters. Thke a look in this House right now. I recognize that the debate is being televised but the odds of a debate in the House of

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
Commons being covered on a substantive matter is fairly limited.
We know who owns the media in this country and we know that most of the media supports the North American free trade agreement and that the media is an ally of this government. It is helping to prevent a public debate. That is a pity because I, unlike some other people in this House, do not spend much time harassing the media. I do not think it is beneficial. However I do think the media people are falling down on the job of telling people what is happening in the House of Commons and what is happening with a particularly important piece of legislation.
We are in a situation where it is up to us, when we have opportunities like today on a related matter, to try to talk about what is happening with the North American free trade agreement. It is fundamentally important for the Liberals to show up and vote as they did not do on second reading when 39 of their some 80 members refused to show up and vote on second reading of the NAFTA.
Madam Speaker, I realize that you would be aware that at that particular stage that measure only passed by 19 votes. With 39 Liberals away the measure passes by 19 votes. That situation was unfortunate.
However, it is not only important that the Liberals finally show up to vote against this, but it is important that when we go into the election this year that all Canadians realize that this is the main issue. Yet, there is only one party in this House of Commons that is saying no to NAFTA and no to the free trade agreement. Let us save the future of Canada.
