speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (for the Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
that Bill C-121, an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend another act in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.
She said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be present in this House today for second reading of the government's latest initiative under the green plan, Bill C-121, an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend another act in consequence thereof.
This legislation forms a part of the marine environmental emergencies response strategy announced in June 1991 and will accomplish a number of tasks. For instance, the bill will oblige the private sector to fund further improvements to marine spills response capability, increase the maximum fine for polluters to $1 million from $250,000, and authorize the adoption by Canada of the international convention on oil pollution prepared-
May 12, 1993

ness, response and co-operation and the international convention on salvage.
As members of this House know, the public review panel on tanker safety and marine spills response capability in its November 1990 final report made 107 recommendations, some with far-reaching policy implications, concerning Canada's ability to prevent and respond to marine spills.
Not all of the panel's recommendations have required new legislation, and the government has taken action to address the majority of the panel's concerns. For example, after July of this year Canada will require that new tankers operating in Canadian waters have a double hull or equivalent design feature, and that existing tankers be either retrofitted or phased-out on an established schedule.
Among other things, the government has also increased the level of foreign vessel inspections, expanded aerial pollution surveillance of the east and west coast and improved training programs. Despite this progress, some tasks cannot be accomplished without new legislation.
For example, the panel pointed out that the greatest risk of oil pollution damage to our waters comes not from Canadian ships but from vessels of other nations. That is the reason it has stressed the need for greater international co-operation and a more effective international regime for prevention of and response to marine spills.
This legislation will permit Canada's accession to the international convention on oil pollution preparedness, response and co-operation, also known as the OPRC convention. This convention which Canada helped develop and is committed to implementing will help ensure greater international co-operation for response to major marine spills.
This legislation also addresses the need for international rules on salvage which better reflect the need for protection of the marine environment. Both international and Canadian marine law concerning vessel salvage have traditionally been based on the principle of "no cure, no pay". Under this principle, salvors are only entitled to a reward if their efforts to salvage a vessel are successful. Unsuccessful efforts, no matter how skilled
Government Orders
or diligent, receive no compensation whatsoever, and no consideration is given to the protection of the environment.
This legislation will implement as Canadian law the provisions of the international convention on salvage, and will effectively change the centuries-old principle of "no cure, no pain" by providing for special compensation for salvors whose efforts succeed in preventing or minimizing pollution damage.
The salvage convention will greatly enhance marine environmental protection. I am proud to ask this House to bring into force a mechanism which will, in the words of the public review panel on tanker safety:
Encourage salvors to prevent, minimize or clean up pollution.
Neither the OPRC nor the salvage convention has yet entered into force internationally. Canada therefore has an opportunity, by being among the very first countries to ratify these conventions, to lead by example, hastening the day when they become part of international marine law.
While this legislation will indeed strengthen the international regime it is concerned primarily with the protection of the marine environment through improved domestic spills response capability.
This legislation will introduce a new regime for responding to oil and petroleum spills that places the responsibility for clean-ups where it belongs, with the polluter. Ships and designated oil handling facilities will be required to pre-plan for spill response and enter into arrangements with private sector funded response organizations to respond to any spills that occur. Plans will have to meet standards set by the government, which will closely monitor private sector response to spills.
It should be said that these new improvements are being made in a spirit of partnership with the private sector and as a result of two years of extensive consultation with the industries affected.
This partnership approach to improving spill response will result in a regional capability for response to spills of up to 10,000 tonnes, and a national capability for response to spills of up to 25,000 tonnes. Those are the very figures recommended by the public panel review.
These are not hypothetical improvements. This legislation clearly sets out government and industry's respon-

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
sibilities and provides for severe penalties for those potential polluters who do not pay and do not comply.
In addition to putting the responsibility for spill preparedness on potential polluters, this bill strengthens the government's ability to ensure swift and effective response to oil spills. If a ship, oil handling facility or response organization proves incapable of mounting a response the minister, through the coast guard, can and will assume control of the response and take any action necessary to prevent, repair, remedy or minimize oil pollution damage. We will also expand the powers of our pollution prevention officers, who form Canada's front line defence against marine pollution.
In the future, the minister's costs for directed cleanups may be recovered from the ship-source oil pollution fund, which will in turn recover costs from the polluter. This new system will ensure that the cost of clean-up does not impede the immediate and effective response.
We will also quadruple the maximum fine for pollutant discharge offences to $1 million and provide for the jailing of marine polluters. Those who would, for profit, endanger the marine environment will learn that this government means business.
We will also provide for greater flexibility in sentencing polluters, as recommended by the public panel review. This legislation introduces a set of guidelines which may be used in imposing a sentence.
The public review panel also suggested a variety of sentencing options beyond imprisonment or fines, such as requiring polluters to publish information relating to the conviction or contributing to research. This legislation will empower the courts to direct convicted polluters to take any action that the court considers likely to prevent the offender from committing the offence again.
I should add that the penalties I mentioned previously are in addition to a shipowner's civil liability under the Canada Shipping Act for costs and damages arising from a ship-source oil spill.
In closing, allow me to reiterate that Bill C-121 is an important element of the government's response to the
public review panel's report, and clearly demonstrates both the government and the private sector's commitment to a cleaner, safer marine environment as well as a sound and prosperous economy.
We must put these measures in place and continue the work described by the public review panel in the title of its final report, that is the work of Protecting Our Waters. Therefore I would call upon my hon. friends opposite to join in a constructive debate and deal as quickly as possible with this very important legislation.

Madam Speaker, I am sure the minister will agree that we always try to engage in constructive debate, particularly on matters of transport and especially where issues such as public safety or the environment are concerned. We try to make useful contributions both in terms of process and substance. I am sure that in the case of Bill C-121 her experience will be the same as we attempt to deal with this in an expeditious manner.
Just after New Year's Day this year the world was horrified by the destruction of a ship, The Braer, off the coast of the Shetland Islands, as once again a huge quantity of oil was spilled on an ecologically sensitive region of the world. We observed on television the scenes of devastation to the environment and the wildlife. We saw the birds and the fish that were entrapped in the oil slick that followed the destruction of that ship.
It was very sobering for all of us to realize that at the same time the sister ship of the The Braer was in Canadian waters and did experience mechanical difficulties and, second, that the The Braer itself was destined for Canadian waters on that voyage. The destruction occurred as a result of mechanical failure on the ship followed by it being tossed against the rocks by high seas. It was an experience that could easily have happened a short few hours or days later off the coast of Canada. This is exactly the kind of disaster that led to the public review panel on tanker safety and marine spills response capability that was referred to a moment ago by the minister. It reflects the very serious concerns that were felt in Canada and elsewhere as a result of the Exxon Valdez disaster which produced a similar result off the coast of Alaska.
May 12, 1993

The Brander-Smith review panel produced a very lengthy report with many recommendations. I think it is fair to say that only a few of these recommendations are being acted upon in this legislation. That is not necessarily meant to be a criticism of the legislation, it is to say there is a great deal more to be done.
The legislation essentially focuses on the very worthy matter of what do we do in the event of a spill? What is the response? How do we build a response capability? How do we pay for it?
The bill contains provision for the creation of response capability in Canadian waters funded by private commitments, by those who transport goods in our waters, especially oil. The result should be the creation of a genuine response capability in Canadian waters. So far so good.
The issue that is not dealt with directly in this legislation and which is raised to such a great extent in the Brander-Smith report is the more important, in many ways, objective of prevention of accidents occurring in the first place.
The comments of the review panel with respect to inspections of tankers and other vessels in Canadian waters I think are very instructive. I will take a moment to refer to the Brander-Smith report beginning at page 22 where the panel writes:
Given the inherent risks of transporting oil and chemicals in Canadian waters, it is imperative that all tankers, both Canadian and foreign, be seaworthy at all times. With cost-cutting in the shipping industry, planned preventive maintenance and inspections risk becoming less of a priority to tanker owners. Tinkers with aging and deteriorating structures and equipment are an unwelcome invitation to disaster. This can only be averted by aggressive vessel inspections and prompt detention of tankers in port for repairs when they do not meet Canadian or international standards for seaworthiness and pollution prevention.
In 1988, the Coast Guard inspected only 8 per cent of the foreign vessels entering Canadian ports. According to the Coast Guard, most of its inspection resources (up to 90 per cent in some regions) are presently committed to conducting compulsory inspections. Under the Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control, to which Canada is a co-operating party, Canada is now committed to inspecting 25 per cent of all foreign tankers visiting Canadian ports. (The results of these inspections will be stored in an international data base and shared with European nations, who will also inspect 25 per cent of foreign tankers visiting their ports.
Government Orders
The report goes on to recommend:
3.3 That the Canadian Coast Guard inspect every foreign tanker on its first visit to a Canadian port and immediately increase inspection levels to 25 per cent of foreign tankers in accordance with the port-state agreement, significantly increase tank barge inspection levels and apply the strictest interpretation to all regulations related to vessel condition and seaworthiness and detain substandard vessels as a deterrent.
The report in perhaps its key recommendations creates a proposed system of economic incentives for the improvement of the vessels travelling in Canadian waters.
What Brander-Smith recommended in essence was a $2 per tonne charge on single hulled vessels which were sailing in Canadian waters to be reduced on vessels that were single hulled but double bottomed to 50 per cent of that charge and of course eliminated on double hulled vessels. We do not see the use of this kind of financial incentive in the legislation although it is clear that the objective of moving toward double hulling is part of what is sought to be achieved.
The question of course is timing and whether the financial incentives to double hull provided in the Brander-Smith report, recommendation 3-2, are essential to creating the environment which we are seeking.
I would also like to point out that we are dealing with a piece of legislation very late in the parliamentary cycle, as we are all aware. Indeed the minister's closing comments reflected that. We have been asked to deal with this legislation in a very expeditious way. I suppose in the interests of seeing that something gets done rather than nothing it is not an unreasonable request. I would like to point out to the House that the response to the Brander-Smith report was so slow in coming that it even provoked commentary in the 1992 report of the Auditor General of Canada. He said, and I am quoting from page 582 of that report: "Cabinet directed that a detailed response to the panel's recommendations be prepared by the end of 1991. As of mid-August 1992 the response had not yet been sent to cabinet".
The lack of a substantive response was still the case this January when we were watching those scenes of devastation from the Shetland Islands.
Admittedly what we have in this legislation is an attempt to balance a variety of interests. Any time you try to bring conflicting interests together in order to

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
arrive at a consensus takes time. I suggest that the House and the people of Canada would have been better served if we could have had this legislation at an earlier point in the parliamentary calendar so that there would have been sufficient time for the legislative committee to study thoroughly the submissions that I expect will be made both by the industry that is affected, by environmental groups and by other Canadians who have viewpoints to express on this important issue.
We are really left with a Hobson's choice. If we insist that full hearings be held, we risk this bill not being passed through the House of Commons and the Senate in time for it to become law before the election. We all know that it could result in a year's delay by the time the whole thing can be reintroduced and put before a new Parliament.
Our choice is this. Do we insist on hearings, or do we expedite the bill, as the minister has suggested we should, in order that it be passed into law before the election?
I suggest this is an unsatisfactory situation we find ourselves in with such important legislation. It is an indication that perhaps this bill sat too far down the government's agenda for too long, provoking negative and what must be very embarrassing commentary by the Auditor General, finally culminating in this bill which can be fairly described as something of a half measure.
That being the case, I think it is important to indicate that we are anxious to see it go to committee and study be commenced as rapidly as possible. We will not try to delay it for any reason other than to make the few comments I have made. I know my colleague from the New Democratic Party will have some comments and my colleague, the member for Davenport will be saying some things. We do want to get this into committee so we can have it studied. Perhaps it is meritorious that it be passed as expeditiously as requested. We will see when we hear what the witnesses have to say.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to debate Bill C-121 dealing with the very broad question of ship pollution.
As I was listening to the comments of both the Minister of State for Transport and my counterpart in
the Liberal Party, the images of tanker collisions, of boats being swamped, of oil, bunker crude spilling over the oceans, the seas and lakes came to mind. I think all of us have watched with horror the devastation, whether it is the Shetland Islands, in Alaska with the Exxon Valdez or even in small amounts on our own shorelines.
The difficulty any government will have is arriving at a solution that works. Too often those of us who are at home watching on TV will say the ships should have double hulls or they should not let crude oil be moved by tankers.
If we were to say that in Canada, if we were to decide as a nation that we did not want any oil moving into or out of Canada by ship that would not stop it because we are surrounded by international waters. Whether it is the Atlantic or the Pacific or the Great Lakes, while we can decide that certain things will occur within our jurisdiction, like air pollution, water pollution knows no boundaries.
We have to recognize that we cannot ban it. The best we can do is control it. I agree with my colleague who says that the ideal is to work to find a way to prevent the spills from happening in the first place.
In part the government's actions are doing that when it comes to decisions related to the type of equipment that the crude is carried in, whether they be double hulled, double bottomed, or compartmentalized. The government has put in process an international agreement which provides that any new vessels being purchased to serve in Canadian waters will have to be double hulled. A process has been put in place that parallels roughly what the United States, our neighbour to the south and a country that shares much of our international waters, has done as well as other governments, to provide for a phase-out of the equipment that is in place or a retrofitting to ensure that the risks encountered are much less.
Ultimately it comes down to decisions made by the owners of the oil companies or the shipping companies in terms of the kind of weather they travel in, the kind of condition their vessels are in. What we have in this legislation is a way to ensure that those who are creating the threat will bear the financial responsibility not just after the fact but all the time the threat is there.

May 12, 1993
I believe by putting the onus on the private sector, the carriers of the crude, to pay to have in place the facilities to clean up a spill is a good step in the right direction.
That is what this legislation does. It requires all of those that have the potential of polluting our waters, and it is not just those ships that carry large quantities of crude oil or fuel, transporting it from A to B to be used by somebody else, but also includes those ships whose own fuel, its own motor power, is a fuel that can spill and does spill. The government has worked to achieve a level of fairness, and I give it credit for that, to ensure that the bulk of the cost will be borne by those who provide the greatest risk in terms of large quantities while at the same time ensuring that those other carriers which I am told actually contribute more in terms of the number of spills have their fair share accorded to them as well.
My colleague from the Liberal Party rightly commented on the length of time it has taken to get to this point. I guess one of the frustrations that all of us as politicians have, not just those in government, but those of us in the opposition, is the length of time it does take. It is a trade-off between accepting a report as in the Brander-Smith report and automatically implementing it. I guess the other extreme is not doing anything at all.
In the middle is that balance in terms of taking a document where hard working, knowledgeable people have come up with a solution, a direction, a blueprint, but like the blueprints we have to then turn to the engineer who can translate them into something that works. The frustrating part is the length of time that that does take.
I guess the real test of the consultation that the Coast Guard and the government have gone through with the industry, with the marine community, with the oil and gas community and dare I say it, the environmental community, is the kind of response we get when we get into committee. Will we have the cruise line operators coming before us and saying: "I'm sorry it is not fair for us to have to pay a subscription fee". Although that amount has not been established it has been suggested that it will be in the magnitude of $300 to $600 or $700 a year as their cost to participate in this program. Will they come forward and say that is too much? They certainly will not come forward and say that it is not enough
Government Orders
because every group these days wants to keep its costs as low as possible.
On the other hand we are told that the shipping industry itself, the tankers, have bought into the concept. In fact they have argued: "Let us do it. Let us have some control over it". Will they come in and say the price is still too steep?
Will the environmentalists come in and say: "Its not good enough. It doesn't provide the protection we want on double hulls or the other elements. It doesn't provide the kind of response we feel is appropriate in the event of a major spill". That will be the test of the consultation that the Coast Guard and the government have gone through.
Again, that is the balancing act. Take the time before legislation to get it right and then when we get to committee, get to the House we find that it is acceptable to the vast majority and all we really do is fine tune. Certainly in this bill nobody disagrees with the principle, the principle being to keep our waters cleaner and to provide a mechanism to clean them up in the event of a spill.
One of the key elements in the bill is similar to legislation that this House passed dealing with the transportation of hazardous goods. That is broad ownership in the plans to deal with a spill. It is not just company x which says to the Coast Guard: "Here's how we are going to clean up this mess if we happen to have a leak". They have to develop a plan. They need to have someone who is prepared to implement that plan. They need to have insurance to cover themselves. They also have to get people to sign off on that plan. They have to get the municipality or municipalities whose shoreline is involved in that area to agree to the plan in the event of a spill as well as the First Nations who are also in the area, the Harbour Commission, the Port Authority, perhaps the railways, perhaps the owners of land; a broad base of ownership of the action plan. That is a very strong element in this legislation.
The bill does a number of other things that I think makes much sense. It provides flexibility and it eliminates some of the unwieldiness of the existing legislation that prevents an individual like myself whose beach front property has been contaminated by ship source oil pollution. Currently I cannot go for any direct help. Under this legislation I can go to the fund and I can be

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
reimbursed as long as it is veiy evident that the pollution comes from a ship. There is some good flexibility in the legislation.
It gives a broader scope for remedial action. The minister talked about the flexibility in sentencing. We have seen incidents provincially in Ontario where instead of just a fine being levied on a pulp and paper company, the court ordered it to provide a scholarship in environmental studies at a local university. There are innovative long term ways of dealing with the problem while at the same time punishing the person who polluted but benefiting society in the long term by channelling that money into education.
There are a number of things such as that in the bill. I do not want to take that much time. We look forward to having it in committee. I think there is some fine tuning we can do.
For example, we need to make sure that when a company advises the minister through the Coast Guard of who the insurance agent is or who is insuring the cargo, there also has to be some mechanism for that insurer to advise the Government of Canada in the event of non-payment of that insurance.
We have seen situations very recently where Transport Canada through the National Transportation Agency was notified by an insurer that an air carrier no longer had coverage. The NTA then pulled the ticket. We need to have that kind of mechanism in place.
The other area I think we need to improve on is the follow up to the bill. We know it is going to take a couple of years for this bill really to be up and running in terms of the applications on the ground, developing the plans, putting in place the responses.
Let us have a mechanism that says in a couple of years from now that a report be prepared, not a very elaborate one, I do not want to have bureaucrats spending six months of their life just trying to prepare for a three-page report, but some kind of progress indication to the House of Commons through the minister, perhaps formally passed on to the transport committee to then evaluate the progress to date.
Then there could be some kind of regular reporting with perhaps a formal five year review, not going off to a commission. I do not want to spend more taxpayers'
dollars, but maybe there could be a formal requirement that the Minister of Transport report to Parliament on the impact of the legislation with perhaps recommendations for changes and that the matter be referred automatically to the appropriate standing committee of this House.
At that time, quite frankly, we could decide whether it would be the Standing Committee on the Environment or the Standing Committee on Transport or any other standing committee that made sense. Let us put in place a mechanism that allows that to occur so that we do not just have Question Period to use to try and push the government of the day, we have another mechanism that will assist parliamentarians in representing the people who elect us.
I look forward to having this bill in committee. My caucus, my party do support it. We support the principle of this bill at second reading. We want to see this bill completed in time to receive royal assent before we not only disappear for the summer but perhaps a lot of people disappear forever from the the political scene as we go into a general election.
From our side we will have one more speaker just so the House knows in terms of the timing for other bills today. I thank you for your attention.

Mr. Speaker, I have a two-part question for my colleague who does an excellent job in the portfolio of transport. The first question flows from his last remarks.
I agree with the member very strongly that it is important for the minister to understand that this kind of legislation very much needs at least a five-year reporting clause that is statutory. I think the public understands that this can in fact be done without requiring a gigantic bureaucracy. Basically one must focus the minds of the Coast Guard and those people in Transport Canada to get the necessary information into an understandable form so it can go into an annual reporting form.
I was pleased to hear my colleague talk about that. I would like to hear from him whether or not he thinks the government side is likely to move on that. They have shown some interest in doing that. We have that kind of statutory reporting requirement in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and others.

May 12, 1993
The second question is in relation to fines. There is one thing that troubles me very much with the many jurisdictions and many fingers that we presently have in the pie. There is the Canada Ports Act and all kinds of jurisdictions. It troubles me that the courts have not taken spills very seriously in the last decade. Between 1979 and 1988 the average fine under the Canada Shipping Act was $4,700. Sometimes the damage done to the environment has been in terms of millions of dollars. Sometimes there was irreparable damage to birds, fish, wildlife and the near-shore environment.
I would like to hear from my colleague on an amendment that I think would be useful and that has now been accepted in principle in terms of other legislation before this House in the recent past. It is to have basic floor fines so that the courts understand how seriously legislators take these kinds of incidents because it is in fact the small spills and the avoidable spills that are doing the greatest amount of damage both in our salt water and fresh water environments. Many judges are unaware of how severe and how widespread the damage can be from a spill in a system like the St. Lawrence where it can float for days. It cleans out birds and surface-feeding fish and kills all kinds of near-shore biota and even deep water organisms.
I would like to hear from my colleague on these two points. First, there is the importance, to this place and to the Canadian public, of having an accurate, regularized reporting process. Second, there should be some floors put in on these fines so that judges start handing out fines that are comparable to the impact of the offences.

Mr. Speaker, in terms of the review we have had a number of experiences. The member makes reference to one. of the decision making on that to say that it would have to happen after three years.

That is why I suggested initially that at the end of the first two years the department gives us even a very simple list: "There are seven plans in place. Here is where they are. Mr. Speaker, it is good to put on record the letter that the panellists of this public review panel on tanker safety and marine spills response capability wrote when they produced this report in September 1990.
We are debating today for second reading a bill which is called an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend another act in consequence thereof. It is a very important bill. It is a clean-up type of bill which attempts to remedy after the fact. In that letter the three panellists-and I am just quoting two sentences-wrote: "As we travelled throughout Canada we were shocked by the extent to which our coastal and inland waters are polluted. It is one thing to read about isolated problems in the comfort of home, but quite something else to witness first hand how seriously many areas are polluted. Pollution from oil and chemical tankers and barges to date has represented a relatively small part of industrial pollution, but in many environmentally sensitive areas even a little could be disastrous. In these areas a major oil spill would be one of the greatest environmental catastrophes this country has ever seen".
Further down, in the forward, the panellists wrote: "It is deeply disturbing to see our waters being polluted by tanker operations especially since much of the pollution is preventable". Please make a note of this observation that much of this pollution is preventable. "At the same time it is extremely difficult to recover oil or chemicals once they have been spilled into the water. Accordingly, we are emphasizing prevention".
It is inevitable that in light of this letter by the panellists that in addressing a bill which is a clean-up bill one would also ask where the prevention policy is. At the same time one would also ask why it has taken two and three-quarter years almost since the production of this final report in September 1990 to have this bill in the House and just for second reading.
It is disturbing, therefore, to note that the speed with which the government proceeds on matters related to
the environment is comparable to that of a snail. It is inexcusable that two and three-quarter years have gone by since this report was produced and that it is not accompanied by a policy measure that is strong on the preventive side as recommended by the panellists.
We are proceeding now at last with a clean-up type of legislation but we are still in a vacuum as far as strong preventive policies are concerned.
There are some measures in this bill that we find very good. I will refer to two of them in particular that flow from recommendation 5-3 of the panel report entitled Protecting our Waters. This is a very fine work that was produced by very dedicated Canadians in consultation with people in various communities and walks of life. The clause being proposed in this bill says:
that Canada should ratify the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in order to encourage salvors to prevent, minimize or clean up pollution.
This convention is now four years old and it is high time that we do subscribe to it in order to protect waters that come under our jurisdiction. That clause in the bill which comes very early in the text is most desirable.
the Canada Shipping Act be amended to make ship owners responsible for any reasonable measures taken by any person to prevent, minimize or clean up the damage, and "Good Samaritans" be protected from suit in the event their well-intentioned actions cause further damage.
This is also a good feature in this bill. There are, however, a number of proposals contained in the report Protecting our Waters that have not been implemented. Some of them could be implemented by being dealt with within the scope of the regulations. Therefore we do not know which they would be. I hope that the minister, if she has not done so already, will clarify that point for us.
Some will not be put into effect. There was a measure which we on this side of the House thought was and is extremely important. It is one that would permit an individual citizen to take action in the courts against the polluter.
It is one of the recommendations contained in Protecting our Waters that would have gone a long way in strengthening the preventive measures. It is regrettable that that measure did not find its way into legislation.
Second, recommendation 5-15 says:

May 12, 1993

In reading the legislation very quickly I came also to the enforcement part of it because it is important that we do have legislation that is not only in the books but is also enforced. It would not be desirable because of cuts and the reduction in government spending to have beautiful legislation which is not enforced because of a lack of personnel.
In section 11 reference is made to disobeying a pollution prevention officer and the consequences that one would incur by doing so. The reference to a pollution prevention officer prompts me to ask the government how many pollution prevention officers will be appointed in order to implement this legislation?
In light of the reduction of departmental operations and budgets, how well will this piece of legislation be implemented? Obviously there is a need to mean what we say to put into effect not only the spirit but also the letter of the legislation. Giving powers to pollution prevention officers is a good step. We welcome that.
It would be distressing and very disappointing if the budget of the Department of Transport did not make sufficient provision for an adequate number of pollution prevention officers. We will follow the estimates of that department very closely to find out how strong that particular arm of the department is in implementing this bill once it is proclaimed.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa South said, we have a difficult decision to make because we see the merits of the legislation in part, but we also see its shortcomings. We are faced also with a very short legislative timetable. As he quite rightly put it, having a Hobson's choice before us, we have to come to the conclusion that it is better to proceed with what is being proposed right now. If we do not proceed we will be left with nothing in hand and the cause of better measures for the clean-up of polluted waters will suffer as a consequence.
The major point one has to add to this discussion is the recommendation made by the panellists that a levy of $2 a tonne be introduced on all oil and oil products transported in Canadian waters and that this levy be used to pay the ship source oil pollution fund, SSOPF. This proposal would have gone a long way in providing a fund for that purpose. I quote from the text of the government response away back who remembers when: "The
Government Orders
economic impact of introducing the levy at the rate of $2 a tonne as recommended by the public review panel will be studied". Evidently it was studied so intensely that it was dropped in the end.
It is a bit unnerving that emphasis is placed on such a narrow interpretation of the word "economic" because one could argue and successfully I submit that in the long term, but even in the short term, the economic impact of such a levy would actually be advantageous because of its preventive effect. The government of the day would send out the signal that by collecting this levy it was serious not only about the clean-up but also about ensuring that those in the industry took sufficient precautionary measures to ensure that the consequences of mishandling and mismanagement would not multiply causing subsequent and further major economic costs.
Therefore it is this narrow approach as to what will be the cost of the levy to a particular commodity and not the approach to the totality of the environment that causes enormous distress. It would have been much better to accept the recommendation of the panellists and introduce this levy which would have meant a very small increase at the retail level. Considering today's price of gasoline and other fossil fuel commodities, it would have made a minimal difference. Canada enjoys unusually low costs for fossil fuel products, particularly petroleum, so the imposition of a $2 a tonne levy is of minimal impact.
It is time for the government to begin the adoption of economic instruments for the purpose of protecting the environment and preventing spills, particularly because this very same government does not believe in the regulatory process. This recommendation of the panellists falls squarely and well within the four comers of the Conservative Party philosophy, namely less regulation but more economic instruments and measures that are either encouraging or discouraging.
I am sure everyone is familiar with the fact that the adoption of economic instruments for encouraging proper behaviour in societal activities is gaining momentum and importance outside Canada. We are still at the stage of examining the instruments that may be available. Despite the paper or catalogue published a year ago by Environment Canada, we have not yet reached the phase of adopting economic instruments for the purpose of protecting the environment. The panellists came forward

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
in September 1990 with a good recommendation and it is most regrettable it has not been adopted.
As my colleague from Ottawa South has said, we look forward to reinforcing this bill in committee, possibly introducing amendments, particularly one that would implement the recommendation made by the panellists on the action that individual citizens can take in the hope that it will not be ruled out of order. It will certainly not add a cost to the legislation. We hope it will be possible to at least advance it and to secure support from government members. Then perhaps the bill will come back enriched by a number of amendments flowing from the Protecting Our Waters report, which has not yet seen its way into the legislation but could still be brought in to reinforce the quality in the public interest and the environment at large.

Mr. Speaker, members in this House will recall it was at the beginning of this Parliament that a panel was ultimately struck to look into the matter of oil and chemical spills in Canadian waters. It followed hard on the heels of the Exxon Valdez disaster in Prince William Sound just to the north of my constituency and also the Nestucca spill which took place in southern British Columbia. It also caused considerable ecological damage, although nowhere near the havoc of the Exxon Valdez or the more recent Shetlands disaster which has had impacts far inshore as a result of the oil moving in the wind stream onshore.
The last time we saw a major move in terms of a compensation fund and legislation to deal with it was following the Arrow disaster in 1970. Canada adopted a maritime pollution compensation fund which was originally gathering funds at a rate of 15 cents per tonne on oil moved to Canada or moved in Canadian waters. A considerable amount of money accrued into that fund.
I regret today to report to the House that the money from that fund has been robbed and has been spent by the Crown. There should be in excess of $200 million in that fund. Instead, as we find in the briefing materials prepared by the Coast Guard and others, the concern the administrator now has is that any expenditure made in a legislative response to that fund will increase
Canada's deficit. It was hardly the constitutional grounds upon which the original compensation fund was set up.
I am also saddened to report to the House that on looking at the more than 20-year history of that fund, almost no funds have been made available to compensate for damage done to fishermen's nets, to beaches, to the ecology, to the bird populations, to fish, to whatever. The funds simply have not been made available.
One of the improvements in Bill C-121, as I have learned from the Coast Guard, is that the administrator will now be able to accept direct representations from the public who arrive and advise the administrator that either oil or chemicals have arrived on their beaches or in their water systems and damage has occurred and certain costs have been incurred to clean that up. The administrator will then pay. I take the Coast Guard at its word that in fact that is what will happen. They do not need to go to court. They do not need to find a court of comparable or necessary jurisdiction to go through the long tangled web of legislation presently available for redress of these kinds of issues by Canadians.
There is a good move inside, but a very sad anecdote to the history of the compensation fund that was set up. Because there are still outstanding issues, some which predate the 1970s legislation, the problem with the Irving Whale. There are other problems endemic within the Canadian jurisdiction of spills, small and large, that have taken place that also have not been addressed.
The majority of our problems of oil and chemical spills are not the gigantic, headline grabbing, get it on the news every hour kind of spills. They are the preventable, smaller scale spills that take place during the day-to-day loading and off-loading operations of tankers large and small and also of the myriad of activities that Canadians and Canadian industry are involved in near our salt and fresh water systems.
The test to put this kind of legislation to is the viability of the response. How good is the government's response to the public review that was appointed by Canada's Prime Minister on June 9, 1989, a wise move by Canada's Prime Minister? The report came back October 24, 1990. Chaired by David Brander-Smith with the able assistance of Denise Therrien and Stan Tobin it produced the report Protecting Our Waters and had 107 principal recommendations. Let me deal for a moment with the
May 12, 1993

major findings and my analysis of how the government has responded.
It is quite clear that cabinet and the Minister of Transport decided not to go with the kind of model the panel had analysed as being the best way to go. That was to put a $2 per tonne levy on oil moving in Canadian waters. That would have provided a very substantive core fund for dealing with the various changes the panel discovered were necessary and are still necessary today to protect the Canadian environment from the transit of oil.
Instead of doing that, instead of taking a direct levy which would come to the Government of Canada and provide for all of the issues related to double hulling, research and development, enforcement, training, guidance systems and so on, cabinet decided to go with the private sector approach. The principal transit corporations of oil would gather the funds through their own form of billing for service. There was the assumption, particularly in relation to oil spill clean-up response equipment and materials that over a very short period of time they would gather together the necessary kinds of response equipment for large and small spills in the Canadian environment.
That is a great deal of trust to place in organizations that have demonstrated, as we learned with the Exxon Valdez, the most recent Shetland disaster, the Kurdistan, the Arrow and the Nestucca, a near-total inability to understand the sensitivity of the ecology or the public rage when spills that could be contained are not and spills that could be cleaned up are not.
Photos are imprinted on all our minds of birds trying to swim to shore covered with oil, whales covered with slicks, fish dying and so on. They are terrifying images for Canadians young or old.
Let us look at the major findings of the panel. First, the capability to respond effectively to a spill of any significant magnitude does not presently exist anywhere in Canada. That was reported in October, 1990 and that statement is still true today.
Government Orders
I spoke to the Coast Guard today and in the whole of Canada at the moment the Coast Guard has only $60 million worth of clean-up equipment. It is spread all the way from the Atlantic, across the Arctic and out to the Pacific coast. We could not deal with a significant spill.
This kind of legislative approach regrettably does not provide for a front-end cash loading from the private sector that benefits enormously by not having the $2 per tonne levy. Let us not forget a $2 per tonne levy works out to only one-tenth of 1 cent per pound, less than 1 cent per gallon tail-end to the user. That is not very much for someone to pay at the pump to know that state of the art response mechanisms capacity and enforcement have been put in place.
It is a decision of less than 1 cent a gallon and that is why I call Bill C-121 the negligent one-cent approach because we have been negligent in terms of the 1 cent. We have opted for it, Parliament has had this put before us and it is better than nothing. It has a skeleton there but we have to put great trust in those oil companies and those delivery companies to live up to their end of the bargain.
I warned them here today that as parties in this House pass on this trust to them, well placed or not, they are receiving it. Should there be a spill large or small anywhere in Canada, if they do not respond and properly contain it and clean it up the media will come back and look at today's debate.
It will reflect on the fact that this Parliament made a judgment. Environmentalists and non-environmentalists in this House decided that at least this was a step forward. We do it with trepidation but we trust that the private sector companies will adequately build themselves in this case.
If the old regime was still in place they would pay at least 35 cents a tonne and more than $2 a tonne under the panel recommendations. It will not be a wait and see. They will not spend the money necessary at their own corporate peril.
The people will not stand by. This time they will cut up their cards from Exxon or whoever ends up being responsible by not having put state of the art technology in place.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
Hulls, onloading and offloading equipment and state of the art guidance systems will be the responsibility of the government. State of the art response and clean-up will be led, administered and researched by the Coast Guard but funded and managed on a day-to-day basis by the private sector.
The second major finding is that each year based on current levels of tanker traffic Canada can expect over 100 small oil spills, about ten moderate spills and at least one major spill. A catastrophic spill of over 10,000 tonnes for which we are wholly unprepared can be expected once every 15 years.
The hour glass is running. It has been four years now since the panel but there has not been one jot, one tittle, one major move ahead by the Government of Canada. Here in the last breathing moments of this Parliament, Bill C-121 is brought screeching red hot from the press to the floor of the House.
I would not be so crass as to suggest that it was solely for electoral purposes knowing that at least in British Columbia, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec, the Northwest Territories and Yukon this is one of the hottest environmental issues going. The government knew it was about to fly into a major maelstrom for having delayed, dithered, dickered, dawdled and dwiddled for so long. Mr. Speaker knows what dwiddled is.
The third major finding is that the risk of spills is highest in eastern Canada, particularly Newfoundland. Placentia Bay is considered by many to be the most likely place in Canada for a major spill with gigantic numbers of transits going back and forth. It is regrettable that I could not find out from the Coast Guard today what the date of retirement is going to be for our tanker fleet which is entirely single-hulled. We know that we can go double-hulled. The majority of our tankers are in the freshwater systems. We know we could at least doublebottom. Certainly we are tied into the Marpole findings and the Marpole regulations. This legislation is so important and has had so many years to be developed, where are the standards and regulations?
This governing party has a terrible habit of bringing legislation to the floor of the House with no standards or regulations even when it is already drafted. This, more
than most pieces of legislation, is standards and regula-tions-driven. The teeth of the bill are in the regulations.
I know ministers who are present recognize that it is a regrettable habit that ministers and departments get into too often by saying: "Keep the regulations back. They may be controversial. Let us just get through with the core skeleton. Let us get through second reading, get it into committee and then maybe we will be safe for an end run around Parliament from there".
It is only because of the importance of getting some legislative initiative going that I am brought to endorse this rather barren and potentially dangerous approach to protecting our environment.
The fourth finding is that a much greater volume of oil enters the marine environment as a result of routine tanker operations such as loading and offloading, tank washings and waste water discharges than of accidents. Almost all of these operational spills can be avoided. This is why I am calling on the Minister of Transport. I do not think members of the House need to fight, scrape and grovel to get an amendment to this legislation for floor fines, not ceiling fines. Let the judges and the courts decide on that.
The overwhelming majority, almost 80 to 90 per cent of the spills degrading and denigrating our environment are from preventable human error or conscious human decisions. It is quicker and easier to just dump it in Lake Superior, dump it in the Vancouver harbour or dump it in the Bow River. Yes, Mr. Speaker, dump it in the Bow River. That is happening.
I think we should make the courts abundantly aware that legislators are very tired. I am sure someone will ask me a question, Mr. Speaker, so I can continue speaking, you know that.
We have discovered floor fines in the area of wildlife and endangered species. Judges and lawyers who might have no idea of the importance placed in the dangers and harm to the environment suddenly wake up when they see there is a $20,000, or $50,000 or $100,000 floor fine for spills of certain thresholds. I agree with my colleague, our transport critic, that we have to have thresholds tied to floor fines.
The average age of our tankers in Canadian waters right now is 17 years and only 8 per cent of the oil tankers operating world-wide have double hulls or bottoms, despite the overwhelming evidence that this type of
May 12, 1993

construction offers a substantially higher margin of operational safety.
We should have learned a lesson on this continent following the Exxon Valdez disaster. There is a tanker operating now off the Queen Charlotte Islands where my home is within sight of Haida Gwaii. It is the Philadelphia and on two occasions it has burst its rivets, started to break up and dumped Alaskan crude into the Pacific waters right off my constituency.
Was it taken out of service? No. Was it ever double bottomed? No. Why not double hulled? As the panel found for a tenth of a cent a pound, for less than a cent a gallon, we could have gone the whole ball of wax and had our environment secured.
One thing I am pleased to see is that our seriously under- resourced Canadian Coast Guard has been able to get on board more vessels with inspection and surveillance. They have managed to get aboard 38 per cent. Regrettably what we are finding is that gigantic numbers of vessels coming into Canada and transiting Canadian waters are in serious need of repair. They are terribly defective. We are finding that the companies are not fixing them.
There is not an adequate level of punitive pressure to make the large oil companies and the transit companies realize they are in violation of Canadian law and that maybe they should change the hull design. Maybe there should not be sleeping or impaired people running the vessels. Maybe they should take a whole new look at what is happening to the earth's environment. If one talks to people like Jacques Cousteau you do not have to listen too long to realize that the major oceans of this world are becoming gigantic septic tanks because of the dumping of fossil materials into the oceans. They wash their tanks on the way back from deliveries. They dump that scrub oil into the water. I think this legislation could have and should have gone much further.
I am sure one of my colleagues in the House will want to ask me a question about that so I am glad to resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the member for
Government Orders
Skeena. I share many of his views in terms of his approach to this proposed legislation.
I want to relate to him an incident that happened to me just last weekend in my constituency office. A group came in to visit me from an organization called Bioquest.
I do not know if you have heard of Bioquest. They are remedial specialists and they have a formula called the Oppenheimer formula. This is a formula that was developed by Dr. Oppenheimer from Houston, Texas, who was the great-grandson of Dr. Oppenheimer who invented the bomb.
This formula has been approved in the United States of America. In fact just recently a bill was passed in the state of Texas called the spills bill whereby any tankers or any kind of traffic in and out of the ports related to Texas have to carry on board the Oppenheimer formula. When the Oppenheimer formula is mixed with a spill it creates a fish food. It is basically a remedial measure for disasters such as the type the member cited.
My question is whether he has heard of the Oppenheimer formula from Bioquest and does he think this is the kind of organization that should come to committee. Some of the ideas that our American friends to the south have are good ideas. If it has worked well for them and has been approved maybe it is something we should look at and introduce into our regulations.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend for that important information he brings to the floor of the House. It is precisely those kinds of responses that should be evaluated by the Coast Guard in relation to this legislation to make sure that as they are evaluating what the private sector is doing with the funds they are generating from those that are transiting oil, very often in dangerous waters and through dangerous environments. If this is demonstrated itself to be useful under a variety of common environmental conditions that we would find here where if there were a small or moderate spill, even perhaps a large one, the Oppenheimer formula might well be introduced at a time when the oil is still reasonably well contained.
We know that the use of a lot of the soap-based and detergent-based tests that have been done, including those done in Prince William Sound, had a more negative impact particularly as they got to the beach than did steam, scrubbing or anything else.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
It is astonishing how terrible the condition of the beaches still is where the oil from the Exxon Valdez came ashore in Prince William Sound. Something that causes a more rapid biodegradation of these fossil compounds near the surface of the water breaking them down into components that could be activated by the phytoplankton and on by the zooplankton and on into the food chain as fish food would be a far preferable impact than going ahead and scrubbing the hell out of the environment, which is what often happens with detergents and the more common approaches taken by the major oil companies so far.
Tied in to my friend's question, members would be interested to know that foreign tankers pose a far greater threat to our shores than do domestic tankers. Almost one-quarter of the foreign tankers inspected by the Canadian Coast Guard in the Atlantic region over just an 18-month period ending in December 1989 were found to be defective. That is an incredible statistic. That is during this Parliament. One-quarter of the tankers were tested. It was during that period. Only one-quarter of the tankers were even boarded and one-quarter of those were defective.
Can you imagine if we checked the entire fleet what the statistic would rise to. Even though we are getting on board more I do not think yet we are getting to the bottom of all of the statistics.
There are two things that are absolutely mandatory. First, under this legislation, and I would hope that the minister brings this before the House as an amendment, once the bill is statutory, particularly as the regulations and standards are added on, that there be a mandatory five-year or less reporting period to Parliament to make sure that the department considers this.
The second is in terms of floor fines. I know my friend has another question to put but I would think that hon. members would be interested in one other point that the panel report found.
Some 62 recommendations designed to minimize the risk of ship-source marine spills are put forward. They deal with environmentally safer vessels, enhanced navigational support, increased inspection, surveillance and enforcement and more competent crews. The Minister of Transport recognizes that improvements in these
areas could reduce marine ship-source pollution by approximately 80 per cent.
Here is where it fell apart and this is what the House has to consider. The Canadian Coast Guard believes that the level of compensation available on the ship-source oil pollution fund is not adequate. That is now. We are being asked to buy into a piece of legislation which would take several years to get up and running. We have only $60 million worth of response equipment in the whole of Canada. We are being asked to let the private sector put all of these materials together and get out there and respond to spills, large or small, between now and the time they are fully up and running.
We have been left with a four year hold by this government with no move and now we are being left with another one. That is an incredible statement about this government particularly after it pilfered and pirated the $200 million to the last penny. The Minister of Finance has drained every last penny out of the oil spill response fund for this country while he has been in office. That is a shameful state of affairs.

Mr. Speaker, this party likes to co-operate with the government when it is doing something reasonable and positive from my perspective and that of others who have spoken this afternoon, particularly when it is actually doing something concrete to move protection of our environment and, more important, to move forward the whole concept of sustainable development.
It is a little difficult to do that today with any enthusiasm. As the debate started in the House the briefing on the legislation was still half an hour away from being completed. I admire the cleverness of the hon. member for Ottawa South, our critic on transport, on the background he has been able to gather to comment with some coherence and conciseness on the bill.
May 12, 1993

The report on the Exxon Valdez spill and the implications of that spill for the safety of Canadian waters and the safety of Canadian shipping was presented in October 1990. The report was done with great thoroughness but very quickly because the authors of the report recognized the urgency of the situation. Interestingly enough, they did not entitle their report "What to do about oil spills". They entitled their report "Protecting Our Waters". That is an issue for Canada as for perhaps no other country in the world. We have the largest coastline in the world. We have the largest concentration in the Great Lakes of fresh water in the world. We have an obligation not only domestically, not only continentally, but to the world to protect that water.
I will quote a former Minister of the Environment in Quebec speaking to a group of members of Parliament yesterday afternoon saying that:"As oil, diamonds, minerals were the precious resources of this century and the last century, the precious resource of the next century will be water".
I will quote from a presentation by Mr. Jim MacNeill before the environment committee yesterday, talking about water but talking about more generally how we respond to threats to our environment. I will quote from . the record of that meeting. He said:"We see that the scale of ecological disasters has continued to rise in the last few years. The famine in Africa ecologically based is greater than any previous famines. The last oil spill off the Shetlands was bigger than the Exxon Valdez. Water shortages are growing. The fisheries collapse. We have experienced a collapse on the eastern coast of Canada and elsewhere and these are without precedent. These things are growing and hope in this scenario lies in the prospect that these ecological disasters will be of sufficient scale to command attention, build awareness, build a demand for action, force action before the disasters become irreversible".
As I say, this report was tabled in October of 1990. We are debating this bill which is at least in part a response to this report and only a partial response to this report in a vacuum because the government's response to the Brander-Smith report, the government's total overview of how it proposes to respond to the type of tragedy that
Government Orders
the Exxon Valdez spill was, has not yet been tabled in this Parliament, over two and a half years after the report was done.
We are told that there are things out of this report that are not in this bill to date because they are being done by regulation or by policy or because they are being done in some other way. We cannot be expected to judge the adequacy of this bill against what needs to be done to prevent another Exxon Valdez spill, to ensure that we can respond to spills and clean up the damage after the fact if and when they happen. We cannot possibly judge the adequacy of this bill except in the context of other measures that the government claims to have taken.
One assessment I can go back to is that of the Auditor General last year in commenting on the Brander-Smith report of 1990-and this was in 1992-how inadequate the government's response had been to that time. He said:"For instance the Coast Guard is seriously under resourced and cannot provide the level of monitoring, inspection and surveillance required to adequately protect our waters. Despite the fact that it commits most of its inspection resources to compulsory inspection and that Canada is a signatory to an international agreement requiring the inspection of 25 per cent of all foreign tankers entering its ports, only 8 per cent of foreign tankers are inspected". This is from the Auditor General's report of 1992, not that long ago.
The Auditor General went on to comment on the many ways in which the government had not met the recommendations of the Brander-Smith report. Of Canada's 31 tankers only one is double hulled and ice reinforced. There is nothing in this bill that states that in a certain period of time that problem will be gone and we will have the protection of fully double-hulled and ice-reinforced vessels.
We will be going into specific recommendations and a discussion of where this legislation falls short in committee. The point I am trying to make is that it is very difficult for us at second reading even to debate the principle of this bill because we do not have the basic information on how adequately this bill, in the context of all other actions that can and should be taken, helps us prevent another Exxon Valdez spill.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
I hope and trust the government is not going to be rigid about dealing only with the technicalities of this bill, that if it is inadequate there will be a great openness on behalf of the government to complete the bill, to do those things which would give Canadians reasonable assurances that everything is being done to protect their waterways, their wildlife, their wildlife habitat, and all those things that are damaged when a terrible disaster occurs. Just as important is whether this bill is adequate to prevent what happens day to day when bits of chemicals and oils leak or are deliberately flushed into our waterways. I do not think so, but it would be nice to be standing here debating it having had the opportunity to find out before the debate began.
The government said in a briefing this afternoon that there are regulations which are now under review, that there are regulations which have been put in place. We know that the primary tendency of this government has been to get rid of regulations. We know that a major review is now going on in all departments to eliminate regulations. We know that review is based on dollar factors and not based on protection of the environment. Environmental regulations in the Department of the Environment are under review to see how many can be got rid of.
To ask Parliament and Canadians to depend on regulation by this government to protect our waters is asking for a leap of faith that I think most of us are not prepared to take.
The government, and particularly the Minister of the Environment, has said a great deal about the impact Rio has had on our development of policy on the treatment of the environment. He has talked a great deal about the importance of the Rio way. He has said that it must be open and must be inclusive.
The government spokespersons were not able to provide any reassurances in the briefing this afternoon that there has been consultation with those environmental organizations and I am not even sure what kind of consultations have taken place with the industry. It certainly has not been the open, inclusive process-my goodness, isn't that a word we are hearing a lot these days-that the Minister of the Environment has said will be the government's way.
As far as I can tell from papers provided by government spokespersons this afternoon the only thing that has been done is to keep people informed. That is not what the Minister of the Environment is talking about when he talks about the Rio way, but maybe it is all talk.
I wanted to talk about another commitment of our famous green plan made over two and a half years ago, a commitment that every policy that went before cabinet would be accompanied by an environmental assessment and that when the policy was tabled, and I presume a piece of legislation is policy, an environmental report concerning the implications of that policy would be tabled at the same time.
I have not seen that and I would really like to see it. I would ask the government if it would please table that. Or has it abandoned the policy of the green plan?
The other thing we will want to look at very carefully in committee is how much in terms of resources will be provided to implement this legislation. We all know that Mexico has some of the best environmental legislation in the world. We also know that Mexico has some of the worst environmental problems in the world. Legislation is just a piece of paper unless the human and financial resources are there to ensure that the legislation is effective.
The Auditor General and the Brander-Smith report made it clear that Canada lacked both the technological resources and the human resources to protect its waterways and clean up damage when it happens. To date we have no assurance that has been corrected. Two days after the Brander-Smith report, after the Exxon Valdez spill, the Auditor General reported a great inadequacy of resources.
There is a great deal to discuss in committee on this legislation. I hope we will have the whole context and the freedom to do that. I cannot help being somewhat cynical and suspicious about whether there is really an intention to get a good piece of legislation through this House before the election.
Perhaps I could close with the words of the minister of fisheries in June 1991. My goodness, it was nearly two years before we had this legislation. He said:
May 12, 1993

For millions of Canadians, our oceans, rivers and lakes are a way of
life. They have supported our communities, commerce and culture.
When they are threatened we are threatened.
I do not think we have a piece of legislation that adequately deals with that threat. We are in the difficult dilemma of deciding whether to support some improvements knowing that they are inadequate or hold the feet of this government to the fire and say: Do what needs to be done. That is what Canadians demand. That is what we think this Parliament should produce.
Is the House ready for the question?
