subtopic: NATIONAL ROUND TABLE ON THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE ECONOMY ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak very briefly on this particular bill. It is a great pleasure for me to recommend third and final reading of Bill C-72, an act to establish the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy.
As the hon. member for Macleod stated, all members of the committee he chaired to review this legislation enthusiastically and unequivocally endorsed passage of the bill. This approval is subject to some minor amendments which have the effect of strengthening or clarifying some sections.
Permit me to say at the outset that the government wishes to thank the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, both members of the opposition, who were most co-operative, supportive and helpful in the deliberations of the legislative committee.
I would also like to formally acknowledge the compelling testimony before the committee of Mr. Ron Doering, the executive director of the round table.
The challenges facing the round table are formidable. Nothing short of moving toward new ways of thinking about the relationships between the environment and the economy is required. This will by definition entail fundamental and profound changes in decision making in all sectors and levels of society from government, business and labour to the household.
Round tables have been Canada's principal institutional responses to the challenge of sustainable development. These innovative multi-stakeholder organizations have taken root in all provinces and territories as well as at the national and municipal levels.
Although progress can seem slow, especially when fundamental change is at stake, Canadians can be proud of this proliferation of sustainable development round tables since their institution was recommended in 1987. That recommendation was made by a multi-stakeholder task force set up by the former Canadian Council of Resource and Environmental Ministers to follow through on the landmark report produced by the Brund-tland commission.

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
As we find in Bill C-72, the mandate of the national round table is to:
Play Ihe role of catalyst in identifying, explaining and promoting in all sectors of Canadian society and in all regions of Canada principles and practices of sustainable development.
It does this by conducting research and analysis, advising governments and other sectors on sustainable development issues and promoting greater public awareness of the economic, social, cultural and policy changes required to move toward sustainable development.
Its membership is diverse, with representation from business, labour, academia, aboriginal peoples and environmental groups, and federal and provincial ministers regularly participating in their plenary or board meetings. Many of these groups are typically in conflict with each other but the round table is an indispensable device in attempting to bridge the gaps that exist between them.
Progress toward sustainability requires new kinds of lateral and integrative thinking that embodies cross-disciplinary, cross-jurisdictional, and cross-temporal perspectives.
As the Brundtland commission forcefully argued:
Those responsible for managing natural resources and protecting the environment are institutionally separated from those responsible for managing the economy. The real world of interlocked economic and ecological systems will not change; the policies and institutions concerned must.
The national round table is one more important response to this challenge, and the federal government is firmly committed to the enterprise. Bill C-72 eliminates the ad hoc, temporary nature of the round table's existence which will enable it to more effectively play its catalytic role in stimulating the new kinds of thinking I have described.
Also very important is the fact that legislated status will permit the round table to organize itself administratively and to conduct its operations in a more efficient manner.
These very brief remarks are concluded when I ask all members to endorse this legislation, as amended. We wish the round table every success as it pursues important activities such as examining the linkages between trade, the environment and sustainability, post-Rio follow-up, reporting on progress toward sustainability
and acting as a catalyst in defining sustainable development strategies for sectors such as pulp and paper.

subtopic: NATIONAL ROUND TABLE ON THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE ECONOMY ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are glad to see this bill go forward, considering the fact that it has been languishing on the Order Paper for some time. But we have to recognize, despite the very eloquent intervention by my colleague from Regina-Was-cana, that it is going forward in a policy vacuum. One has to conclude, and regretfully so, that the government knows how to spell sustainability but it certainly does not know how to implement sustainability.
I will in the time available bring forward a number of examples to prove this. First of all, there is no domestic energy policy in this country. Members will appreciate that the national round table has been given the assignment to integrate the economy and the environment. In order to be effective it would need an indication from the government which way it intends to go on this extremely important policy sector, namely energy. It has been proven over and over again that energy is an important component of any policy that declares itself to be sustainable in relation to climate change, climate warming and the impact of energy production on the environment in general.
We see this absence not only in the field of energy. There is no domestic policy on transport. We know that good, efficient ground transportation in urban centres as well as inter-city ground transportation makes an enormous difference in improving the quality of the environment, and therefore in enhancing increasing sustainability.
We have no water legislation yet in the House, although it has been promised since 1987. Therefore we have to conclude that the government has no long-term views on what should be the water policy for Canada. We do not yet have water quality legislation in the House.
We do not have and we miss veiy badly the fact that we do not have any urban transportation whereby Ottawa would provide general long-term guidelines and goals for the well-being of Canadians living in cities.
Another area where we do not have an international policy is that related to development aid. We did have one and I thought it was a relatively good one, but recent cuts and recent statements made by respected ministers have demonstrated that CIDA's policy is no longer one of development aid but one of commercialization, one of turning that agency into a self-serving commercial insti-
May 12, 1993

tution which will in large part exploit developing countries for Canada's commercial interests.
That is why this bill, while desirable, goes forward in a policy vacuum. That is an observation which must be made at this point. I am sure that the member for Skeena will have some interesting remarks to make on this aspect as well.
What we witness when it comes to any discussion or assignment of the kind given to the national round table through this bill, namely of bringing together the economy and the environment, is a growing gap. There is a gap between declarations, between statements, between declarations of intent, if you like beautiful speeches at the United Nations or at Rio on the occasion of the UN environment conference, but when it comes to the application and implementation of policies at home that would integrate, that would mesh, that would bring together the economy and the environment for the long-term interest of our natural resources and our human health and well-being in general, then we will see a lack of action, we see a growing gap. Studies, reports, round tables if you like and declarations do not see their translation into action as one would expect.
I will give you an example. The Prime Minister went to the Hague to attend the summit on the protection of the global atmosphere. This was March 11, 1989.1 will quote a few paragraphs from his statements at that time on behalf of the Canadian people. "Our presence today in the Hague is an expression of a common aim. The earth's atmosphere is deteriorating. To counter the threats posed we are here to demonstrate a common strength of purpose and to seek solutions". A good statement.
"The heads of state in government present here are demonstrating their courage by moving to a new stage in the fight against atmospheric pollution". A good statement.
"The leaders present here are putting their names and reputations behind an act of determination, determination to make our fight against the deterioration of the earth's atmosphere more effective". Fine.
Government Orders
"Now is the time to call for an accelerated evolution of the international institutions dedicated to control atmospheric pollution".
Now we look at what the Government of Canada is doing or has done since that time in reducing greenhouse gas pollution, the emission of carbon dioxide in particular. We see that four years later the Government of Canada has no plan in place to prevent global climate change. It has no plan.
It is no wonder the public has become disenchanted and cynical with politicians because statements are not supported by subsequent actions. This is one example.
The Government of Canada did announce one year after the Prime Minister's statement in the Hague that it intends to stabilize-it is not a great decision but nevertheless it is a first step, better than nothing if you like-carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2000. It did so in 1990. Yet today three years later we do not have that plan.
How can one explain, how can one justify this inaction? South of the border President Clinton announced in April of this year, just four weeks ago, the intention of the United States to stabilize the emissions of carbon dioxide gases by the year 2000 and to produce a plan five months later, by the month of August of this year.
One wonders why should Canada be so hesitant, so inconclusive. It is four years after the Prime Minister's statement in the Hague, three years after the commitment that was made in Canada to stabilize emissions and we do not have a plan. So much for sustainability as far as the energy field is concerned. We can find other disturbing elements that must be put on record in this debate because we hope that by doing so the National Round Table will at least receive signals from parliamentarians who in the end are expressing here the views of Canadians at large and perhaps be able to put together a policy paper for the consideration of the government.
Also I do not think that should be the sequence in the process. The government should actually indicate to the Round Table what it intends to do in order to ensure long term sustainability of the economy and the environment. Having done so, it would ask the National Round Table

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
then to act on that broad and general but nevertheless important policy framework and proceed with that.
We read instead little items like this in the press the other day: "The federal government and Canada's forest ministers will spend $6 million during the next three years helping the forest industry polish its tarnished image overseas". What is going on here? If it has a tarnished image then go to the root of the problem to find out why it has a tarnished image. Probably it has to do with the devastating clear-cut operations on the west coast. Improve the image by way of improving the operation of that industry rather than spending $6 million on public relations.
Coming to federal-provincial relations, we learned that the Canada-Ontario agreement respecting the Great Lakes, which is an extremely important water body on which some 8 million Canadians and Americans-at least in Lake Ontario-depend on, has not been renewed since March 1991. What is this government doing? This kind of agreement is intended to improve the quality of water for the long term and therefore enhance the sustainability of people who depend on that particular and very precious body of water.
We also have to bring into this debate the fact that in February of this year the government proceeded with the abolition of a number of very important councils which had a bearing on the production of policies on sustainability. These were: the Science Council of Canada; the Economic Council of Canada; the ocean institute and a few others. They have been actually abolished as part of the deficit cutting operation.
Only a few weeks ago the Minister of Finance, coming to transportation, announced cuts to VIA Rail. Evidently this government is moving theoretically and by way of this particular bill, which gives legal status to the National Round Thble on the Environment and the Economy, on a certain track to demonstrate that it has an intention. However, having done so, its actions actually undermine and erode the whole purpose and the whole spirit of the policy thrust, if ever there was one, of integrating the economy with the environment.
Let me bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, another example which I find almost infuriating. Since March
1992 pesticides have been exempted from the GST by virtue of a decree by the Minister of Finance. When it comes to books, no, that cannot be done, but when it comes to pesticides this government finds it politically excusable to proceed in exempting pesticides from the GST. One wonders what kind of thinking motivates and permeates this government when it wants, at least in speeches and through the means of this particular bill, to enhance the necessity and the notion that we should integrate the environment and the economy, and then all of a sudden removes a tax from pesticides. The two do not come together. They do not make sense.
Let us move to another area where there is a policy gap. I mentioned it briefly earlier, namely the one relating to development aid. In the paper entitled Sharing Our Future some three or four years ago, we had a good document published by the then minister in charge of CIDA, in which a commitment was made "to help the poorest countries and people of the world".
At the earth summit last year in Rio when the United Nations held the conference on the environment and the economy, Canada pledged itself with other countries to increase development aid to the nations in need by some 7 per cent of our gross national product which is an increase of almost 30 per cent.
Instead the government moved back at home and decided to cut aid. It cut aid by 10 per cent for a total of $642 million by the year 1994-95. Who is hurt in this process? One will appreciate that when we talk about sustainable development, which is, as I said, the integration of the environment with the economy, we also talk about the poorest countries of the world that are struggling with desertification, with deforestation, with the lack of water and natural resources, with poor health conditions, you name it.
Who gets hurt as a result of these cuts, these withdrawals? Countries such as Tanzania, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Uganda are the countries at the bottom of the barrel according to the statistics produced by the United Nations Development Program. These are the most needy nations and Canada has now decided to phase out and stop certain projects that were aimed at improving the provision of water or the milling of grain or stopping desertification or improving agricultural
May 12, 1993

practices, basically all efforts aimed at improving food security if you like and improving health conditions.
Another policy which I mentioned earlier that also must be raised in this debate is the fact that with the present estimates this government has a policy with respect to energy which runs counter to sustainable development. If one looks at the estimates of the department of energy and if one looks at our taxation system, we come across some phenomenal-for lack of a better word-tax provisions which favour the use and the production of fossil fuels.
Drawing from the last taxation year of 1991, for instance, just the value of tax deductions by the oil and gas industry amounted to some $4.9 billion which was then translated in a loss of revenue of at least $500 million. The tax deduction advantages given to the mining industry are also a substantial figure, which I do not have on hand right now, but they are worthy of at least mentioning.
Direct tax expenditures by the federal government to the energy sector by way of budgetary decisions amount to about $700 million. Of these, only 5 per cent go to research and development of alternative sources of energy, the ones we want to develop in order to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels and therefore reduce carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions. Federal assistance to the energy sector amounts to roughly $1.9 billion which goes mostly to energy projects. The commitments to energy megaprojects at the present time is roughly $4 billion.
In other words, we have the conventional, old-fashioned type of policy making, taxation provisions, budgetary provisions, subsidy provisions, tax accelerated write-offs, you name it, that are unsustainable if you really, by contrast, want to ensure the implementation of policies that one would expect this national round table to implement or to propose to the government.
The round table has existed already for some time. I cannot see how it can function effectively unless the basic and fundamental attitude of the government changes to provide the attitude that is needed at the political level for the national round table to function effectively.
Government Orders
I have concentrated for a moment on energy policy because it is easier to find the subsidies and the tax incentives that are made available under present policies. I can assure the House that if one were to find the time, one could find also unsustainable tax advantages and subsidies in the fields of transportation, agriculture, forestry and maybe still in the field of fisheries.
This brings to mind the social and economic drama on the east coast where really for the first time Canada faces a very serious problem of unsustainable fisheries for which the warning had been given in early 1990 by Dr. Harris when he indicated in a report that the cod fishery was in severe danger.
We cannot say when we speak about sustainability and sustainable development that we lack practical examples. On the contrary, we have one right at home in the fisheries. If we do not watch it, we will have examples we can draw on in forestry, particularly in the cutting of the old stands on the west coast. We have to understand that it is not very responsible or very politically wise, if we are here to promote the interests of the public, to give lip service to sustainable development, the integration of the economy and the environment and create the impression that we have the instruments to do that while in reality we do not.
By way of a last example, let me bring forward one that was even the subject of a vote in this House on March 9 when a vote took place on Canada ratifying the Law of the Sea. That vote was in the negative because the government decided that it should not support a motion that we put forward which would have given a parliamentary green light to the executive, namely cabinet, to finally ratify the Law of the Sea Convention. Keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that Canada was one of the first nations to sign it in the early eighties, but an international convention first requires signature and then ratification.
While Canada was one of the first nations to sign the Law of the Sea Convention in the eighties, Parliament is now against passing a motion in favour of ratifying it.
The Law of the Sea Convention requires 60 nations to ratify it. As we speak today, some 55 or 56 nations have ratified it already, so four more are needed to make it

May 12, 1993
Government Orders
operative. It would be a great pity if it becomes operative without Canada being part of it.
Why am I using this example? Because the Law of the Sea has many concepts in it for sustainable fisheries. Articles 63 and 65,1 believe, are extremely important for the sustainable management of fisheries in international waters. We want that. It is in the interest of our own population.
There seems to be some international interest related to the mining of the seabed and we seem to be influenced by other nations to hold back and not ratify this extremely important convention. It is waiting to be implemented in the interests of increasing and enhancing the potential for sustainable management of fisheries in international waters.
Mr. Speaker, I hope with this analysis I have given you a picture that there is some deception going on here which has to be raised.
In committee within the scope of the bill, we managed to pass a couple of amendments which will probably strengthen the mandate of the institute. We certainly did our best to give it every possible means to operate better and more effectively. For instance, we modified its mandate so it would be able to advise the government on ways of integrating environmental and economic concepts and policies. That is just one way of saying sustainable development.
We made a provision that would give a mandate to the institute to engage not only in public information but also in the promotion of sustainable development among Canadians. This is a very important role for the round table to perform.
We should not have any illusions that by passing this bill the Government of Canada has embraced the policy of sustainable development and the recommendations that came out in 1987 by the Royal Commission on Environment and Development headed by Madam Brundtland. Canada has been very good at making statements abroad. We performed quite well in Rio in a number of initiatives which are desirable and highly welcome at international levels. But-and this BUT is in capital letters-when it comes to domestic policies and the implementation of what we embrace abroad, we notice a lack of courage, political reality and political will in this government.
It has the capacity to promote and embrace concepts which are popular at the time, but when it comes to the test of moving from theory to practice, from declaration to action, we see a very sad and growing gap.
I regret to have to make these statements at this stage. I would have preferred to be much more positive on the occasion of third reading of Bill C-72, but this thought had to be expressed and put on the record. I am sure the member for Skeena in his articulate way can do much better than I did.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the remarks of the member who just spoke covered a lot of the waterfront of the problems that the National Round Table has faced and continues to face. I know time is short, so I will try to compress my remarks to ensure this legislative mandate that has been long sought by those associated with the National Round lable gets underway.
It is sad that considering the time it has taken for it to get here the government side could not find a minister of the Crown to give it the kind of government will this legislation should receive on third reading, so all those who volunteer their time to the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy would know that all parties stand four square behind the concept of the institution.
Until we go a lot further than the rhetoric associated with sustainable development, we will continue to go the wrong way on the face of this planet. It is now five years since I took a tour with members and had hearings right across the country. Canadians made it very clear they wanted at least 1 per cent of the Gross National Product of this country set aside in sustainable development centres where they could go to get the information and tools at the grass roots democratic level that are necessary to implement sustainable development.
It is the actions of individuals on a day-to-day basis that can and will have the largest impact. Ultimately the only way to have a successful impact in terms of sustainable development is to equip individual Canadians and individual residents of this globe with the information and tools necessary to get us from here to there.
May 12, 1993

One of the problems this bill will continue to have after it becomes law is that members are chosen by government and Governor in Council and they are there at the pleasure of the Governor in Council. I think anyone who has participated in it, been present at its meetings or spoken to members who have participated know it is over-weighted on the side of industry.
The Governor in Council should solicit the views of members of the environment committee, members of this House or members of certain academic or other institutions in this country to find people who are at the top of the learning curve on environmental issues. It should place them in there, perhaps even for shorter periods of time, to ensure that the institution operates a critical mass. It should do assessments of full cost accounting of government, energy policy, hydro-electric policy, cumulative impacts, global warming and what we are doing to the ozone.
It has to go into these big fields to make this a relevant national institution and make its membership relevant. Regrettably it is marginalizing itself as an institution, even though it will now have a legislative mandate. It is not going to the heart and pith of the issue of how to integrate environment and the economy and have the real sustainable development that is its mandate. If it continues to take its instructions from the corporate boardrooms and from singular political perspectives, it will continue to fail the people of Canada.
I offer this as unsolicited advice to the present and future membership of the National Round Table. It has my support. It has the support of many Canadians. It now has a legislative mandate. Let us hope it now picks the more difficult issues and gets the Canadian media on side to talk about full cost accounting.
One last point that was raised just yesterday by Jim MacNeill, one of the most notable and wisest environmentalists on the face of the earth is that the 24 OECD countries now squander more than $1 trillion a year on unnecessary subsidies in their economies. It is high time we had that kind of ecological level playing field, full cost accounting and real integration of these issues because without it the four horsemen will ride and will ride soon to all our doom.

MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-294, an act to amend the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Natural Resources envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have a copy here of volume VI of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1985. It is the last published consolidation of the laws of Canada of which I am aware and contains all the laws ever passed by the Canadian Parliament that were still in effect at the time of its revision.
Chapter M-9, in this sixth volume of the Revised Statues of Canada, 1985, is the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act. Nestled snugly in the sixth volume of the revised statues, means it is the law, right? Well, no. It is true the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act was passed by Parliament in 1982. As passed, it grants the federal cabinet the authority to set fuel efficiency standards for any class of motor vehicle it chooses. The standards themselves are to be set by regulation.
Unfortunately, although the bill was duly passed by this House more than a decade ago, it has never come into force. It has never become the law. That bill, as

May 12, 1993
Private Members' Business
passed by the 32nd Parliament, contained an often used parliamentary device, a provision to the effect that it would not come into force and would not become the law until it was proclaimed by the Queen's representative. For whatever reason, it has never been proclaimed. Each successive government has kept it up on the far reaches of the statutory shelf out of commission and gathering dust.
This brings me to Bill C-294, the bill before the House this evening. The bill I am sponsoring, an act to amend the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act, is very simple. If passed, it would result in what is called the coming into force of the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act. That is it. No more, no less.
If Bill C-294 passes, then the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act at long last becomes the law. Until the 1982 act becomes the law, the government still will not have the authority to set mandatory Canadian fuel efficiency standards for cars and light trucks. Instead we will continue to rely, as we have been relying, on voluntary compliance with suggested standards and self-monitoring by the automotive industry.
It is not that the setting of fuel efficiency standards is itself radical or unprecedented, in fact this bill would give effect to the same principle-this time concerning motor vehicles-that the current Parliament approved and implemented last year when it adopted Bill C-41, the Energy Efficiency Act.
Bill C-41 authorized the establishment of energy efficiency standards for household appliances and other energy-using devices. Bill C-294 would complement Bill C-41 by allowing similar standards to be set for vehicles having internal combustion engines.
There is of course a legitimate question which all members of the House might ask themselves at this point. Is this bill needed? Clearly, successive Canadian governments over the past decade have thought not. Were they right? If they were, are they still right?
The answer is no. For a number of environmentally crucial reasons, the answer is that Bill C-294 and the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act to which it would give effect are very much needed right now. Why? In a nutshell, Canada must quickly cap and
then begin to reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases, the most important of which is carbon dioxide.
Bill C-294 is a crucial first step in this process. There is no shortage of evidence that emissions capping and reduction are necessary. The House of Commons Standing Committee on Environment is celebrated in part for the fine study it conducted on the issue of global warming. The committee's report issued in March 1991 called for a 20 per cent reduction in the 1988 levels of carbon dioxide emissions produced by humans and human activities by the year 2005.
As well, the committee suggested the government adopt this goal as "its minimum interim objective in reducing Canadian carbon dioxide emissions". Unfortunately the Conservative government obviously has not thus far adopted this objective. Instead the government has indicated that it plans merely to cap Canadian C02 and other greenhouse gas emissions at 1990 levels by the year 2000.
There seem to be efforts afoot to back away even from this modest goal. For example, the House of Commons Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources issued a report in January of this year that waffles prodigiously saying that such a goal "may or may not be attained". We are talking about the capping goal here. It is suggesting that any financial assistance Canada provides to reduce emissions in other countries should be allowed to substitute for concerted domestic action.
More important, the government has repeatedly taken action which makes it more difficult to meet even the modest goals it has set for itself. For example, the Conservatives keep paring back funding for their much touted green plan. It has reduced funding for environmentally responsible energy efficiency and alternatives programs by nearly 90 per cent from the more than $410 million spent for these purposes when they first formed the government in 1984-85.
In spite of all the government's hedging, stalling and even back-tracking, in spite of this apparent lack of utterly warranted concern, there is just no question that action must and can be taken to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and the other greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
The transportation sector is key. It is an obvious place to start and one of the largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Taking action in this area need not cost a
May 12, 1993

lot of money. I am certain the government would be pleased to learn that.
As an August 1989 report by the federal, provincial and territorial energy ministers put it: "There are substantial opportunities in Canada to reduce the emissions of carbon dioxide at the point of energy use, and they are cost-effective for society, leading to significant dollar savings from energy conservation and improved energy efficiency. No additional economic value needs to be placed on the reductions of carbon dioxide emissions to make them cost effective".
Again these are the federal, provincial and territorial energy ministers speaking. This same energy ministers' report also states that "emphasis should be placed on means to reduce emissions in the transportation sector". They conclude that "Transportation energy use offers the greatest potential for emissions reductions at point of use". Reducing these emissions is precisely what Bill C-294 and the original act to which it would give effect are all about.
According to the comprehensive Environment Canada report entitled Canada's Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Estimates for 1990, ably compiled by A.R Jaques and released in December 1992, transportation accounted for 32 per cent of Canada's total of 461 million tonnes of carbon dioxide by source in 1990. Automobiles and gasoline-powered light trucks alone accounted for over 72 million tonnes, more than 15 per cent of Canada's total 1990 C02 emissions.
One of the best ways to decrease greenhouse gas emissions is to reduce the amount of greenhouse gas producing fuel needed to run our vehicle fleets. Tighter motor vehicle fuel consumption standards lead directly to reduced fuel consumption and thus reduced greenhouse and other gas emissions. It all starts with making Canada's cars and light trucks more fuel efficient. [DOT]
In their recent book Healing the Planet noted environmentalists Anne and Paul Ehrlich emphasized and I quote: "The efficiency of automobiles themselves can be greatly increased. There is enormous potential for further savings, perhaps moving to 60 and 70 miles per U.S. gallon, levels already achieved by European experimental cars such as the Volkswagen Eco-Polo and Volvo's LCP 2000".
Private Members' Business
Canada's Friends of the Earth in 1990 called on the government to set standards that would compel auto manufacturers to improve fuel economy for cars to five litres per 100 kilometres by the year 2000. That is about 56 miles per gallon for us old folks. They estimated this move alone could save 60 million barrels of oil per year by the year 2005 and could by itself reduce carbon dioxide emissions by over 5 per cent of current levels.
Many helpful fuel economy technologies and design improvements already exist. Some of these are described in the recent report by the office of technology assessment of the U.S. Congress, a report entitled Improving Automobile Fuel Economy: New Standards, New Approaches.
These existing measures include weight reduction, aerodynamic drag reduction, front wheel drive, overhead cam engines, four valves per cylinder engines, intake valve control, four and five speed automatic transmissions, continuously variable transmissions, electronic transmission control and the list goes on and on.
It should also be noted and as this report adds later that: "Significant improvement in fuel economy should be possible over the longer term, by 2001, for example, without compromising safety. Over this time period there are opportunities to improve fuel economy without downsizing as well as opportunities to redesign smaller cars to avoid some safety problems particular to them".
Why not simply get on with the job of increasing fuel efficiency? One of the main problems is that the federal government seems to have been content to rely on voluntary fuel efficiency standards. Unfortunately voluntary standards just are not working.
The over-all fuel efficiency of Canada's new motor vehicle fleet increased rapidly during the 1970s, a period you will recall of rigorous regulatory inducement to improvement in Canada and in the United States. It then slowed in the early 1980s and has not improved significantly since then. As a result Canada's fleet of new vehicles are no more fuel efficient over all than they were 10 years ago.
It gets worse. In a November 5, 1990 news release the Friends of the Earth pointed out: "Seven of the 20 largest auto companies in Canada did not meet the company average fuel consumption, the CAFC guideline, in 1989, five years after the guideline took effect. In

May 12, 1993
Private Members' Business
the U.S. these companies would automatically be forced to pay fines and be vulnerable to legal action. In Canada they are violating the target, polluting seriously and have no legal or financial incentive to improve".
Transport Canada officials report that about half the fuel efficiency ratings for new cars, pickup trucks and vans are never audited. Many companies do not even submit the relevant fuel efficiency data to the department.
The U.S. office of technology points out several ways in which in the words of its report Improving Automobile Fuel Economy, "the market is not supporting reduced gasoline use". These are U.S. problem areas. It is safe to assume that trends identified hold broadly true for Canada as well. These include the following:
"Consumers have been turning in growing numbers to less efficient light trucks for passenger vehicles. Between 1970 and 1985 light truck miles tripled while auto miles grew by only 38 per cent.
Auto makers are building and consumers are buying increasingly powerful cars. Average zero to 60 miles per hour acceleration times of the U.S. auto fleet have decreased in every year since 1982 at a cost of more than two miles per gallon in average fuel economy.
Consumers increasingly order options that reduce fuel efficiency such as air conditioning, power accessories and four wheel drive.
New emission and safety standards are likely to have adverse effect on fuel economy.
The growing numbers of autos creates traffic congestion that lowers on road efficiency of the fleet".
Even the Americans have recognized the predictable and prosaic truth. The market alone does not work to increase fuel efficiency.
They are not alone. In the significant March 1989 report entitled "Energy Demand in Canada, 1973-1987" Ottawa's Marbek Resource Consultants emphasized just this point. In the words of that report: "To achieve the major economic and environmental benefits that energy efficiency still has to offer, government policies and programs for the future will need to emphasize a
strategic combination of energy efficiency standards, improved information programs, financial incentives and R & D assistance. To rely solely on energy prices and existing market mechanisms is a formula for failure. Active and constructive intervention in the marketplace is absolutely essential".
Unfortunately the current government seems to be going in the opposite direction. For example, it is cutting information programs. Transport Canada cancelled the 1993 edition of its popular fuel consumption guide which every year, until this year, had provided consumers with fuel consumption figures for every make and model of car, van and light truck sold in Canada. That guide is now gone.
I am the first to admit that relying solely on mandatory fuel efficiency standards is not prudent. They do after all have their limitations. For example, manufacturers do indeed require lead time to improve the efficiency of their vehicles. If not carefully designed, such standards can place unequal burdens on different manufacturers. Mandatory standards alone do not provide for incentives for continuous improvements beyond the legal requirements.
Finally as vehicles become more fuel efficient people tend to drive them more often and farther thereby reducing the improvement's benefits in reducing overall carbon dioxide emissions.
In spite of these limitations however, there can be no doubt that increasingly stringent mandatory standards could have significant salutary effects, but it should not stop there. As Ehrlich and Ehrlich point out, our vision of increased energy efficiency must begin to include a host of additional considerations. These should include things like filling buses and trains instead of commuting with one-person cars.
Even more important is redesigning cities and suburbs to make them pedestrian and bicycle friendly. We should be redesigning cities so that homes for people of varied income and employment levels are near offices, shops, schools and workplaces. All these advances are necessary and will prove tremendously helpful. However, prudence dictates that we must also institute, indeed we should begin with, mandatory fuel efficiency standards.

May 12, 1993

Private Members' Business
Let me conclude by quoting at length from a letter that the president of the Canadian Automobile Association sent to energy minister, Bill McKnight, on April 13 of this year, copies of which were subsequently sent as well to all members.
The association has worked long and hard to improve energy efficiency standards and these are among the observations they made to the minister in that letter:
CAA shares with you and the federal government a concern for the environment, the green plan objectives and your government's commitment to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. We are asking you to proclaim the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act as one important means of achieving those goals. There are many good reasons for taking this action:
This is what Canadians want the government to do. A survey of CAA members asked what steps should be taken to reduce automobile-related pollution, and 83 per cent said they favoured tighter and enforceable fuel economy standards-Better fuel economy is easy to achieve -Canada has international commitments. Not only has Canada committed itself to carbon dioxide reduction targets, but we have played a leadership role among nations-There is a demonstrated need. Without the force of law, the government cannot force automakers to meet current 'targets', let alone tighten those targets-This is just one step that must be taken. Other steps include fuel economy standards for light duty trucks and vans and for heavy duty vehicles, as CAA has already proposed-The green plan's credibility is at stake. With public support and no economic cost or increase in the deficit, this is an easy step the government can take to reduce the risk of global warming and improve the environment.
These are good and wise words that are easily heeded. All that is required to enable the government to act is that the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act come into force. The passage of Bill C-294 would achieve that.
However, we all know that that is not going to happen. This item is not votable. It will die at the conclusion of today's debate unless something else happens. This is why I hope at the conclusion of this hour's debate to rise on a point of order to place before this House an alternative suggestion.
For the time being just let me note that helping effect the coming into force of the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act would be a fine, helpful, forward-looking and, I suspect, substantially non-controversial note on which this 34th Parliament might bow out.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE FUEL CONSUMPTION STANDARDS ACT
speechtext:
As the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources I am very pleased to speak tonight and I would like to wish my hon. colleague from Champlain the very best as the new parliamentary secretary. My colleague from Edmonton East and I have worked together for the last four years. I know that he will not enjoy most of my speech tonight but I certainly have enjoyed working with him.
I would like to point out the factors which they argue for not supporting Bill C-294.
As we know, the automobile industry is important to our economy not only in terms of direct jobs in assembly but also in parts manufacturing, vehicle sales and other associated industries. In addition, Canada has enjoyed many benefits under the Auto Pact with the United States. The actions which affect the operation of this industry must be considered with great care in order to not damage its viability. This is particularly important at this time as the industry-not just the North American industry but the world-wide industry-has been hit hard by the recent recession. We have seen massive restructuring of this sector as a result of this and a leaner, more competitive industry is emerging.
In the matter of setting new standards for the automobile industry, timing is of paramount importance. Over the period 1994-96 the automobile industry has signed on to meet a further round of emission standards that are the most stringent in the world. These are the same standards that are required in the United States under the amendments to the Clean Air Act. This is a challenging task to meet standards that require 98 per cent control of hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions and over 80 per cent control of nitrogen oxides. Beyond this, the industry is developing technology to meet even more stringent requirements for California, including the so-called "ultra-low" or "zero" emission vehicles. There is no lack of technological challenges for this industry.
Technology for better emission control has focused on better fuel combustion by using ever more sophisticated computer control and steady improvements to the catalysts which clean up vehicle exhaust emissions. These are areas of technology in which the North American industry is a leader. However, these technologies are relatively minor in their impact on engineering and

May 12, 1993
Private Members' Business
manufacturing decisions as they affect relatively few components which do not result in changes to the vehicle as a whole.
Fuel consumption technology affects almost every component of new vehicles as well as the over-all design. I need hardly point out the significant improvements in aerodynamic shape of vehicles over the last few years and the change from rear-wheel to front-wheel drive. More difficult to see are the reductions in weight of the hundreds of individual components that make up modern automobiles. These reductions have been achieved by clever design and the substitution of lighter materials such as high strength steels, aluminum and plastics. These changes are not ones that can be made bit by bit to new vehicles on a year-by-year basis. The majority of such changes must be designed into new vehicles from the start, and therefore attention must be given to adequate lead times and the timing of introductions of new vehicle models.
This subject is complex and one in which there are a variety of diverse views respecting the impact of changes in technology on vehicle cost. There have been several recent studies on this subject culminating in the report by an expert committee of the U.S. National Research Council in 1992. This study is titled Automotive Fuel Economy: How Far Should We Go? It points to a range of potential improvements in fuel consumption of new vehicles, but highlights out the uncertainties in cost estimates for new technology. Cost is a critical factor as consumers will not be willing to pay for technology that does not yield adequate returns in fuel cost savings.
The availability of fuel efficient technologies in the Canadian market will depend in large part on decisions domestic manufacturers make about technology they will incorporate in their North American production. This technology menu will be influenced by consumer demand but would be more strongly influenced by any fuel consumption program eventually adopted in the United States.
It is important, therefore, that Canadian fuel consumption requirements do not try to force domestic manufacturers to use technology they would not consider producing for the North American market as a whole. This does not mean that the average fuel consumption of
Canadian vehicles would be identical to that in the U.S. For instance Canadian fuel prices may continue to be higher than the U.S. price. This has a small effect by influencing Canadian consumers to buy a mix of new vehicles that are slightly more fuel efficient than those purchased by consumers in the United States. These differences manifest themselves in more purchases of manual transmissions and smaller optional engines, for example. What is important here is that consumers have a choice of technology options available to them. Restriction of choice leads to less interest in the market and hence declining sales.
This brings me to another important point. Canada cannot easily act alone in the area of automotive standards. Any program requiring significant engineering and design changes must be founded on a common approach to standards setting with the United States. It is not feasible for a country with a relatively small automotive market to act without regard to other markets, especially when free trade is becoming a reality with those markets. The technology contained in individual models for vehicles will be the same. The expense and risk of producing a vehicle with technology different from other markets is too high to be acceptable to manufacturers and more importantly to consumers. Any differences in the markets will be based on consumer preference among vehicle types, and these differences will be reflected in the sales mix of vehicles in the U.S. and Canada.
A further point concerns the design of a fuel consumption program and the necessity of harmonizing program design. Most discussion of new fuel consumption standards has focused on the level of improvement. Just as much attention needs to be given to the form of a new program and the impacts different forms would have on vehicle manufacturers.
Complaints regarding the unfairness of current Company Average Fuel Consumption CADC standards in the U.S. have led to suggestions to change the method of gauging compliance. The current CADC program fixes a single absolute standard that all manufacturers must meet. This type of standard favours manufacturers of small cars while penalizing manufacturers whose product

lines are restricted to large, luxury or performance car markets.
While these are arguments which favoured this design of program in 1975, the market today is very different and it would be advisable to examine the other program options.
Other types of standard programs have been suggested, including those in which different standards are set for different size or weight classes of vehicles, and those which provide for a uniform per cent improvement over a base year.
The debate on alternative forms of standard programs must account for the fact that there are three classes of stakeholders affected by standards, each with a different point of view. They are: the nation as a whole, with social interest in fuel efficiency and environmental protection, the car buyers, and the auto manufacturers. The social interest would be to assure that any form of standard has the following attributes: it is conceptually simple for the public to understand; it can be administered easily and inexpensively; it provides incentives for all manufacturers to offer fuel efficient products; it guarantees fuel consumption improvements in the future.
Consumers have a different perspective as individuals and primarily would like to see the market offer a wide range of attributes desired with no restrictions.
Typically these attributes include interior room, acceleration performance, good ride, safety, efficiency, economy, reliability, durability and luxury features. Standards that would require a degradation of desired consumer attributes or seriously restrict choice are likely to be unpalatable to consumers and this would be reflected in declining sales.
Finally, the auto manufacturers who must comply with standards are concerned primarily with their ability to meet such a standard and whether or not the standards program affects their competitive position. Depending on the level at which standards are set, manufacturers may be unable to comply if the standards are technologically infusible and the type of standard makes no difference if this is the case.
However, if the levels are set at a point where technology feasibility is not a major issues then the type of standard can raise issues.
I know, Mr. Speaker, my time is up. I would like to table the balance of my speech. I know that many Canadians will be very interested in it.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that the government is going to allow this matter to go to committee and that the member who moved it, our colleague from Edmonton, is going to move an amendment that the subject matter of the bill be referred to the energy committee.
On behalf of the Official Opposition I think that is an excellent proposal and I will be happy to second his motion when he gets up in a few moments to move that the subject matter of the bill go to the committee.
Very briefly, the Canadian Automobile Association, which has 3.5 million members-Mr. Speaker, you are probably a member, I am and I am sure the member for Edmonton East is-a not for profit association, has strongly invited I believe members of all parties in this House to support the member's initiative.
I will give a few quotes from the letter, just enough to make the point. This is from Michael McNeil, the president of the Canadian Automobile Association, dated April 13:
We are asking you to proclaim the Motor Vehicle Fuel Consumption Standards Act as one important means of achieving those goals.
He is referring to the reducing of carbon dioxide emissions. Mr. McNeil goes on:
A survey of CAA members asked what steps should be taken to reduce automobile-related pollution, and 83 per cent said they favoured tighter and enforceable fuel economy standards. This compares to 63 per cent favouring more transit spending, just 18 per cent favouring special gas taxes, 54 per cent wanting emission testing programs, 50 per cent asking for car pool lanes and a mere 28 per cent favouring higher parking rates.
He basically goes on to make the following point:
Better fuel economy is easy to achieve. Auto makers oppose this move, as they oppose most attempts at regulation, by saying it cannot be done. However, studies have shown that it can be done without downsizing or compromising safety. Corporate Average Fuel Consumption standards allow the manufacturers to improve fuel economy on various models in the vehicle mix, giving them flexibility on how they achieve the goal.
Mr. McNeil reminds us of Canada's international commitments and points out that failing to act on this issue which has massive domestic support and is technologically feasible will not add a penny to the deficit and the debt that is drowning our children, our grandchildren and ourselves.

Automobile efficiency can also be effectively promoted through point of sale price incentives designed to stimulate consumer demand for cleaner and more efficient vehicles. The gas-guzzler tax is an established mechanism that has been constructive in raising the fuel economy of low-mpg cars, particularly since 1983.
I might point out that in Japan I understand that if one buys what is called a gas guzzler one pays the equivalent of about $600 Canadian per year to have an operator or owner's permit. If one buys a vehicle that is fuel efficient, which is of course what the member is trying to get at in this bill, one pays I am told about $100 or $125.
In that way the Japanese are fighting air pollution. It is the same kind of initiative I suggest that we are dealing with here today. A lot of points have been made, with which I agree, by the member for Edmonton East. I think enough has been said. If I stop talking, Mr. Speaker, then we can all go home, so I will stop talking.

been 8.6 litres per 100 kilometres, instead of 13.1 litres, the latter being the standard in 1978. There has been a vast improvement in the way we monitor efficient energy use in this country.
